Foods originally from the Americas.Tomato: Tomatoes came from the Americas, and Europeans long feared them as poisonous; Italian tomato sauce dates only to the 1600s.

Foods originally from the Americas.Chili pepper: Chili peppers originated in the Americas, and Columbus named them peppers when he mistook them for black pepper.
Foods originally from the Americas.Turkey: Wild turkeys were domesticated in Mexico, and the bird got its name from a muddle with guinea fowl imported via Turkey.
Foods originally from the Americas.Pumpkin: Pumpkins are native to North America, with seeds found in Mexico dating back thousands of years.
Foods originally from the Americas.Peanut: Peanuts are not nuts but legumes that ripen underground, and they originated in South America.
Foods originally from the Americas.Pineapple: Pineapples came from South America, and Europeans named them for their resemblance to pine cones.
Foods originally from the Americas.Avocado: Avocados come from Mexico, and the word comes from the Aztec Nahuatl 'ahuacatl', which also meant testicle.
Foods originally from the Americas.Cashew: Cashews are native to Brazil, and each nut hangs from a fruit called a cashew apple; raw shells contain a toxic irritant.
Foods originally from the Americas.Sweet potato: Sweet potatoes were cultivated in Central or South America by about 5,000 years ago, and Polynesians had them before Europeans did.
Foods originally from the Americas.Wheat: Wheat was domesticated in the Fertile Crescent over 10,000 years ago, in the Old World and not the Americas.
Foods originally from the Americas.Barley: Barley is one of the earliest cultivated grains, farmed in the Middle East for over 10,000 years, long before contact with the Americas.
Foods originally from the Americas.Grapes: Grapes are Old World, and wine grapes were grown in the Caucasus region some 8,000 years ago.
Foods originally from the Americas.Olives: Olives come from the Mediterranean, and olive trees can live for well over a thousand years.
Foods originally from the Americas.Garlic: Garlic comes from Central Asia and was eaten by Egyptians, who found cloves in Tutankhamun's tomb.
Foods originally from the Americas.Onion: Onions are Old World crops grown for thousands of years, and workers on the pyramids were said to be fed them.
Foods originally from the Americas.Apple: Apples originated in the mountains of Kazakhstan, where wild ones still grow, and not in the Americas.
Foods originally from the Americas.Carrot: Early carrots from Central Asia were purple or white, and the orange kind was bred in the Netherlands.
Foods originally from the Americas.Cabbage: Cabbage is native to Europe, and was cultivated by the ancient Greeks and Romans.
Foods originally from the Americas.Black pepper: Black pepper is from India's Malabar coast, and its trade was so valuable that it was once used to pay rent.
Foods originally from the Americas.Cinnamon: Cinnamon comes from the bark of Asian trees, in Sri Lanka and southern India, and once cost a fortune in Europe.

Styles of pizza (not lookalikes).Neapolitan: Neapolitan pizza has UNESCO recognition for the art of the pizzaiuolo. It is baked in a wood-fired oven at about 480°C for roughly 90 seconds.
Styles of pizza (not lookalikes).New York style: New York style pizza has big, thin, foldable slices, and its crust is credited to local water. The first U.S. pizzeria opened in Manhattan in 1905: Lombardi's.
Styles of pizza (not lookalikes).Chicago deep-dish: Chicago deep-dish is baked in a high-walled pan with the sauce on top of the cheese. A single slice can take about 45 minutes of baking.
Styles of pizza (not lookalikes).Detroit style: Detroit style pizza is rectangular, baked in blue steel pans once used for auto parts. Its crispy, caramelized cheese edge is the best part.
Styles of pizza (not lookalikes).Sicilian: Sicilian pizza is a thick, rectangular pie with a spongy base. In New York, it is the square slice on pizzeria counters.
Styles of pizza (not lookalikes).Roman: Roman-style pizza includes the thin, crisp pizza tonda and the rectangular al taglio, sold by weight. The latter is eaten as street food all over Rome.
Styles of pizza (not lookalikes).Grandma pie: Grandma pie is a thin square pie, baked in an olive-oiled pan, from Long Island. It is cooked at home and the cheese goes under the sauce.
Styles of pizza (not lookalikes).St. Louis style: St. Louis style pizza has an unleavened, cracker-thin crust and is topped with Provel cheese. It is cut into squares, called party cut.
Styles of pizza (not lookalikes).New Haven: New Haven pizza, called apizza, is charred and often oblong. Frank Pepe's, founded in 1925, is famous for its clam pie.
Styles of pizza (not lookalikes).Margherita: Margherita pizza, with tomato, mozzarella, and basil, was said to be made in 1889 for Queen Margherita of Savoy. Its colors match the Italian flag.
Styles of pizza (not lookalikes).Focaccia: Focaccia is an Italian flatbread, but it is not usually topped like pizza. It is dimpled and brushed with olive oil instead.
Styles of pizza (not lookalikes).Lahmacun: Lahmacun is a Turkish flatbread topped with spiced minced meat, often called Turkish pizza. It is thin, rolled up with herbs, and eaten by hand.
Styles of pizza (not lookalikes).Pide: Pide is a boat-shaped Turkish flatbread with its edges folded up around a filling. It looks like pizza but has a distinct shape and tradition.
Styles of pizza (not lookalikes).Quiche: Quiche is an egg custard in a pastry shell, a French dish from Lorraine. It is a tart, not a pizza.
Styles of pizza (not lookalikes).Tarte flambée: Tarte flambée is a thin Alsatian flatbread topped with cream, onion, and bacon. It was traditionally used to test the heat of a wood oven.
Styles of pizza (not lookalikes).Khachapuri: Khachapuri is Georgia's cheese-filled bread, and the boat-shaped Adjarian type is topped with an egg and butter. It is breakfast, not pizza.
Styles of pizza (not lookalikes).Piadina: Piadina is a thin Italian flatbread from Romagna, folded around cured meats and cheese. It is a sandwich wrap, not a pizza.
Styles of pizza (not lookalikes).Okonomiyaki: Okonomiyaki is a Japanese cabbage pancake, not a pizza. Diners often cook it themselves on a hot plate at the table.
Styles of pizza (not lookalikes).Naan: Naan is a leavened flatbread baked in a tandoor, not a topped dish. It is dipped in curries and not topped with sauce.
Styles of pizza (not lookalikes).Bruschetta: Bruschetta is grilled bread rubbed with garlic and topped with tomatoes. The name comes from bruscare, meaning to roast over coals; it is a toast, not a pizza.

Styles of pizza (not lookalikes).Tostada: A tostada is a flat, crisp-fried tortilla topped with beans and meat. It is a Mexican dish, not a pizza.
Styles of pizza (not lookalikes).Crêpe: A crêpe is a thin French pancake, folded around fillings. Savory buckwheat versions, called galettes, are from Brittany, not a pizza.
Styles of pizza (not lookalikes).Garlic bread: Garlic bread is sliced bread slathered with garlic butter and baked. It often shows up beside pizza, but it is a side dish, not a kind of pizza.

Types of cloud.Cumulus: Cumulus clouds are the puffy cotton-ball kind that form on warm days, and a typical one can weigh as much as 100 elephants.
Types of cloud.Stratus: Stratus clouds form flat gray sheets low in the sky, and fog is basically a stratus cloud touching the ground.
Types of cloud.Cirrus: Cirrus clouds are wispy ice-crystal streaks high above, often 6 to 12 kilometers up, and can signal a change in weather.
Types of cloud.Cumulonimbus: Cumulonimbus clouds are thunderstorm towers that can reach over 12 kilometers high, and they produce lightning, hail and tornadoes.
Types of cloud.Altostratus: Altostratus clouds form a thin gray veil in the mid-levels, through which the sun looks like a dim disc behind frosted glass.
Types of cloud.Altocumulus: Altocumulus clouds look like white or gray patches in rows, and when they show up on a warm humid morning, storms may follow.
Types of cloud.Cirrostratus: Cirrostratus clouds form a thin milky sheet of ice crystals high up, and they create halos around the sun and moon.
Types of cloud.Cirrocumulus: Cirrocumulus clouds form small white ripples at high altitude, known as a 'mackerel sky'.
Types of cloud.Nimbostratus: Nimbostratus clouds are thick, dark and low, and they bring steady rain or snow, not showers.
Types of cloud.Stratocumulus: Stratocumulus clouds are lumpy gray-white patches that often cover the sky in a low layer.
Types of cloud.Mammatus: Mammatus clouds hang in pouch-like bulges beneath storm anvils, and they look dramatic but are not a sign of a tornado.
Types of cloud.Lenticular: Lenticular clouds form smooth lens shapes over mountains, and they have been mistaken for UFOs.
Types of cloud.Stratosphere: The stratosphere is a layer of atmosphere, above where most clouds live, and it holds the ozone layer.
Types of cloud.Isobar: An isobar is a line on a weather map joining places with equal pressure, so it's a map line, not a cloud.
Types of cloud.Nebula: A nebula is a cloud of gas and dust in space, not in our sky, and some are where new stars form.
Types of cloud.Monsoon: A monsoon is a seasonal wind shift that brings heavy rain, not a cloud type.
Types of cloud.Mistral: The mistral is a cold, strong wind in southern France, and it's a wind, not a cloud.
Types of cloud.Sirocco: The sirocco is a hot wind from the Sahara into southern Europe, so it's not a cloud.
Types of cloud.Tornado: A tornado is a rotating column of air, which might come from a cloud, but is itself a storm, not a cloud type.
Types of cloud.Typhoon: A typhoon is a hurricane in the western Pacific, a storm system rather than a cloud type.
Types of cloud.Aurora: An aurora is a glow made by solar particles hitting the upper atmosphere, and is light, not cloud.
Types of cloud.Troposphere: The troposphere is the lowest atmosphere layer where nearly all weather and clouds occur, but it's a layer, not a cloud.
Types of cloud.Hailstone: A hailstone is a ball of ice that falls from a cloud, but it's precipitation, not a cloud type.
Types of cloud.Haboob: A haboob is an intense dust storm, from the Arabic for 'blasting', and not a kind of cloud.

Scientific laws (not jokey \"laws\").Boyle's law: Robert Boyle found in 1662 that squeezing a gas into a smaller space raises its pressure in proportion. It is why scuba divers must exhale while ascending.
Scientific laws (not jokey \"laws\").Ohm's law: Georg Ohm showed that current equals voltage divided by resistance. When he published it in 1827, many scientists dismissed it.
Scientific laws (not jokey \"laws\").Hooke's law: A spring stretches in proportion to the force applied, within limits. Robert Hooke first published it as a Latin anagram to keep priority.
Scientific laws (not jokey \"laws\").Charles's law: At constant pressure, a gas expands as it is heated. Jacques Charles studied it while pioneering hydrogen balloons in the 1780s.
Scientific laws (not jokey \"laws\").Kepler's laws: Three rules from Johannes Kepler describing planets' elliptical orbits. Newton later explained them with gravity.
Scientific laws (not jokey \"laws\").Hubble's law: Edwin Hubble found that distant galaxies recede faster the farther away they are. It is the key evidence that the universe is expanding.
Scientific laws (not jokey \"laws\").Coulomb's law: The force between two electric charges falls with the square of their distance. It echoes Newton's gravity formula, but charges can repel.
Scientific laws (not jokey \"laws\").Snell's law: It describes how light bends when entering water or glass. It's why a straw looks broken in a glass of water.
Scientific laws (not jokey \"laws\").Pascal's law: Pressure applied to a confined fluid spreads equally in all directions. It is the principle behind hydraulic brakes and car lifts.
Scientific laws (not jokey \"laws\").Newton's laws: Three laws of motion from 1687 in Principia, including 'every action has an equal and opposite reaction'. They underpin classical mechanics.
Scientific laws (not jokey \"laws\").Faraday's law: Michael Faraday found that a changing magnetic field creates an electric current. Every power-plant generator relies on this.
Scientific laws (not jokey \"laws\").Murphy's law: A trap: 'anything that can go wrong will' is a joke, not a scientific law. It's credited to US engineer Edward Murphy in 1949.
Scientific laws (not jokey \"laws\").Moore's law: Gordon Moore noted in 1965 that chip transistors double about every two years. It's a prediction about industry, not a law of nature.
Scientific laws (not jokey \"laws\").Parkinson's law: 'Work expands to fill the time available.' Cyril Northcote Parkinson wrote this in a 1955 essay about bureaucracies, as satire.
Scientific laws (not jokey \"laws\").Sod's law: The British version of Murphy's law, famous for toast landing butter-side down. It's humor, not physics.
Scientific laws (not jokey \"laws\").Godwin's law: As an online argument goes on, the chance someone compares something to Hitler approaches 1. Mike Godwin coined it in 1990.
Scientific laws (not jokey \"laws\").Cole's law: Just a pun: it means thinly sliced cabbage. Wordplay on 'coleslaw', so it's not a law at all.
Scientific laws (not jokey \"laws\").Betteridge's law: Any headline ending in a question mark can be answered 'no'. Journalist Ian Betteridge popularized it in 2009.
Scientific laws (not jokey \"laws\").Hofstadter's law: A task always takes longer than expected, even accounting for Hofstadter's law. Douglas Hofstadter wrote it about chess programs.
Scientific laws (not jokey \"laws\").Poe's law: Without a clear sign of sarcasm, extreme views online can't be told from parody. Named after Nathan Poe, from 2005.
Scientific laws (not jokey \"laws\").Peter principle: People get promoted until they reach their level of incompetence. Laurence Peter's 1969 book made the joke famous.
Scientific laws (not jokey \"laws\").Brooks's law: Adding people to a late software project makes it later. Fred Brooks wrote it in his 1975 book The Mythical Man-Month.
Scientific laws (not jokey \"laws\").Hanlon's razor: Never attribute to malice what stupidity can explain. It's a rule of thumb about people, not a scientific law.
Scientific laws (not jokey \"laws\").Occam's razor: The simplest explanation that fits the facts is usually best. It's a guiding principle named for a 14th-century friar, not a physical law.

Lab safety equipment.Goggles: Safety goggles seal around the eyes to block splashes and flying fragments. Ordinary glasses don't protect from splashes that come from the side.
Lab safety equipment.Lab coat: A lab coat is mostly a barrier against spills, and is usually cotton or a blend. Synthetic coats may melt onto skin if they catch fire.
Lab safety equipment.Gloves: Different chemicals need different glove materials. Nitrile resists many solvents, but some chemicals pass straight through thin latex.
Lab safety equipment.Face shield: A face shield guards the whole face against splashes and flying debris. It's worn over goggles, never in place of them.
Lab safety equipment.Fume hood: A ventilated cabinet that pulls hazardous vapors away from the user. Keeping the sash low improves both safety and airflow.
Lab safety equipment.Eyewash station: Rinsing the eyes for about 15 minutes right after a chemical splash can mean the difference between recovery and permanent damage. Stations are tested weekly.
Lab safety equipment.Fire extinguisher: Labs often keep several types, because water can make chemical and electrical fires worse. Class D extinguishers are for burning metals.
Lab safety equipment.Safety shower: A deluge shower can drench a person in seconds to wash off chemicals or put out burning clothes. It typically delivers a large volume per minute.
Lab safety equipment.Fire blanket: A fire-resistant blanket that smothers flames on a person or bench. It works by cutting off the oxygen supply.
Lab safety equipment.Respirator: A respirator filters or supplies air against dangerous fumes and particles. For it to work, it has to seal tightly, which is why fit testing is a thing.
Lab safety equipment.Bunsen burner: A gas burner, not a protective item. Robert Bunsen's design mixed air into the gas for a hot, clean blue flame, which is itself a hazard.
Lab safety equipment.Beaker: A basic glass container, and a hazard rather than safety gear. Its markings are only rough estimates of volume, so it's bad for precise measuring.
Lab safety equipment.Test tube: Standard lab glassware, not protective equipment. Test tubes are made of thin heat-resistant glass so they can be warmed directly.
Lab safety equipment.Pipette: A tool for moving measured liquid. Mouth pipetting was once common practice before the dangers were recognised, and it's now banned.
Lab safety equipment.Centrifuge: A machine that spins samples to separate them by density. It's a hazard if unbalanced, which is why tubes must be loaded opposite each other.
Lab safety equipment.Microscope: A tool for seeing tiny things, and not protective equipment. The first compound microscopes appeared around 1600.
Lab safety equipment.Petri dish: A shallow glass or plastic dish used to grow microbes, named for Julius Petri, who worked with Robert Koch. It's equipment, not protection.
Lab safety equipment.Scalpel: A very sharp cutting blade, and a hazard in itself. Dissection scalpels often have replaceable blades that need careful disposal.
Lab safety equipment.Burette: A graduated glass tube with a stopcock, used to dispense liquid precisely in titrations. It's measuring gear, not safety kit.
Lab safety equipment.Hot plate: A heated surface for warming solutions without a flame. It's safer than a burner for flammable liquids but can still burn skin.
Lab safety equipment.Spatula: A small tool for scooping powders. It's tooling rather than protection, and each chemical gets its own clean one.
Lab safety equipment.Flask: Conical Erlenmeyer flasks are a lab staple. Their narrow necks make swirling liquids easy, and they're glassware rather than safety kit.
Lab safety equipment.Funnel: A funnel guides liquid into narrow openings. It's a handling tool, not protection, though it does help prevent spills.
Lab safety equipment.Magnetic stirrer: It spins a small magnet inside a flask to mix liquid with no moving parts touching it. It's useful, but it's not safety gear.

Styles of rock music.Punk rock: Punk rock came from bands like the Ramones in the mid-1970s, with songs often shorter than three minutes.
Styles of rock music.Grunge: Grunge came out of Seattle, and Nirvana's Nevermind in 1991 pushed it into the mainstream.
Styles of rock music.Heavy metal: The term likely stems from a Steppenwolf lyric about 'heavy metal thunder', in Born to Be Wild.
Styles of rock music.Glam rock: Glam rock mixed glitter, platform boots and big riffs, with Bowie and T. Rex as key names.
Styles of rock music.Prog rock: Prog rock stretched songs into long suites, as with Pink Floyd and Yes.
Styles of rock music.Indie rock: Indie rock's name comes from independent record labels, and its sound varies hugely.
Styles of rock music.Hard rock: Hard rock turned up the blues-rock guitar riffs, with Led Zeppelin and AC/DC as stars.
Styles of rock music.Psychedelic rock: Psychedelic rock of the 1960s used effects and long solos, with Jimi Hendrix a pioneer.
Styles of rock music.Surf rock: Surf rock is built on drenched reverb guitar; Dick Dale's Misirlou was revived in Pulp Fiction.
Styles of rock music.Garage rock: Garage rock got its name from bands practising in garages; Louie Louie by the Kingsmen is a classic.
Styles of rock music.Post-punk: Post-punk followed punk with moodier sounds, as in Joy Division and Gang of Four.
Styles of rock music.Jazz: Jazz is improvised music from New Orleans, not rock, though rock borrowed some of its freedom.
Styles of rock music.Blues: The blues is rock's parent: early rock and roll grew from it, though it's separate.
Styles of rock music.Reggae: Reggae is a Jamaican style with offbeat rhythm, led by Bob Marley.
Styles of rock music.Disco: Disco is dance-floor music with four-on-the-floor beats, and not part of rock.
Styles of rock music.Techno: Techno is electronic music from Detroit, built on machines instead of guitars.
Styles of rock music.Hip hop: Hip hop began in the Bronx in the 1970s with DJs and MCs, so not rock.
Styles of rock music.Salsa: Salsa combines Cuban and Puerto Rican rhythms, a dance style apart from rock.
Styles of rock music.Opera: Opera is sung drama with an orchestra, and not rock.
Styles of rock music.Bluegrass: Bluegrass is acoustic string music from Appalachia, named for Bill Monroe's Blue Grass Boys.
Styles of rock music.Gospel: Gospel is spiritual music with roots in church choirs, separate from rock.
Styles of rock music.Bossa nova: Bossa nova is a Brazilian mix of samba and jazz, whose best-known song is The Girl from Ipanema.
Styles of rock music.Dubstep: Dubstep is bass-heavy electronic music from South London.
Styles of rock music.K-pop: K-pop is South Korean pop, with polished groups and choreography.

Audio recording formats.Vinyl: Vinyl LPs revolved at 33 and a third rpm, a speed set in 1948. They have made a strong comeback in recent years.
Audio recording formats.Cassette: Philips introduced the compact cassette in 1963 and made the design license-free. It made mixtapes and the Walkman possible.
Audio recording formats.CD: The CD launched commercially in 1982, with Billy Joel's 52nd Street among the first. Its length was said to be set so Beethoven's Ninth fit on one disc.
Audio recording formats.MP3: The format arrived in the 1990s from Germany's Fraunhofer Institute. It shrinks files by discarding sounds human ears barely notice.
Audio recording formats.8-track: These cartridges were hugely popular in 1960s and 70s cars. Their tape loop split songs mid-track with a loud click as it changed programs.
Audio recording formats.MiniDisc: Sony's 1992 format used a small magneto-optical disc. It never beat the CD or MP3 outside Japan and some professional uses.
Audio recording formats.Reel-to-reel: Magnetic tape from Germany's wartime radio shaped postwar music. Studios used it for multitrack recording from the 1950s.
Audio recording formats.Wax cylinder: Edison's cylinders, from the 1870s and 80s, were among the earliest recordings. Early ones could only be played a limited number of times.
Audio recording formats.WAV: A Microsoft and IBM format from 1991 that stores uncompressed audio. It is why a three-minute song is far larger than an MP3.
Audio recording formats.FLAC: It compresses audio with no loss, usually to about half the size. Its name stands for Free Lossless Audio Codec.
Audio recording formats.AAC: Advanced Audio Coding is the successor to MP3 and the default for Apple's music downloads. It sounds better at the same bit rate.
Audio recording formats.VHS: The tape was for video, though it carried sound too. Its 1970s format war was won over Betamax, while the tapes recorded pictures.
Audio recording formats.JPEG: A 1992 standard for compressing photographs. The name honors the Joint Photographic Experts Group, so it is for images, not sound.
Audio recording formats.PDF: Adobe created it in the early 1990s to share documents with the same layout everywhere. It stores pages, not audio.
Audio recording formats.GIF: It has existed since 1987 and is for images. Its inventor said it was pronounced with a soft g, like peanut butter, a contested claim.
Audio recording formats.Polaroid: Edwin Land's instant photography has been around since 1948. It records images, so it doesn't fit audio.
Audio recording formats.Betamax: Sony's video cassette format lost the home video war to VHS. It was a video format, so it does not record audio-only music.
Audio recording formats.Telegram: The telegram sent messages in Morse code and, in the US, was last sent by Western Union in 2006. It is not a recording format.
Audio recording formats.Fax: The fax transmits images of pages over phone lines. It dates back to the 1840s, long before it reached offices.
Audio recording formats.PNG: Created in the mid-1990s as a free alternative to GIF. It stores lossless images and has nothing to do with sound.
Audio recording formats.Microfilm: This compact film stores miniaturized documents, and the technology was used for newspaper archives and even wartime messages by pigeon.
Audio recording formats.Filmstrip: Used in classrooms before video. Filmstrips were often paired with a separate audio cassette, but they carried only images.
Audio recording formats.DOCX: The default file type for Microsoft Word since 2007. It is a zipped bundle of XML files for text, not audio.
Audio recording formats.TIFF: A flexible image format popular with publishers and scanners. It stores pictures, not sound.

Rodgers and Hammerstein musicals.Carousel: Rodgers himself called it his favourite of his works, and "You'll Never Walk Alone" came from it.

Rodgers and Hammerstein musicals.The King and I: Based on a governess's memoir about Siam, it opened in 1951 and starred Yul Brynner, who played the king over 4,600 times.
Rodgers and Hammerstein musicals.The Sound of Music: Their last musical, from 1959, inspired the 1965 film that became one of the highest-grossing films ever.
Rodgers and Hammerstein musicals.Cinderella: Written for television in 1957 starring Julie Andrews, it drew over 100 million viewers when it aired live.
Rodgers and Hammerstein musicals.Flower Drum Song: Set in San Francisco's Chinatown, it was among the first major Broadway shows to have a mostly Asian American cast.
Rodgers and Hammerstein musicals.State Fair: Their only musical written straight for film, in 1945, and the Iowa story later got a stage version.
Rodgers and Hammerstein musicals.Allegro: Their 1947 musical about a doctor's life was an experimental work, and one that flopped.

Rodgers and Hammerstein musicals.Guys and Dolls: Frank Loesser's 1950 musical is built on Damon Runyon's gamblers, and it is not by R&H.
Rodgers and Hammerstein musicals.Fiddler on the Roof: Bock and Harnick's 1964 show, with "Tradition", was the first Broadway musical to pass 3,000 performances.
Rodgers and Hammerstein musicals.Hello Dolly!: Jerry Herman's 1964 hit won 10 Tonys, and the title song gave Louis Armstrong a No. 1 single.
Rodgers and Hammerstein musicals.West Side Story: Bernstein and Sondheim updated "Romeo and Juliet" to 1950s New York in 1957.
Rodgers and Hammerstein musicals.Annie Get Your Gun: Irving Berlin wrote it in 1946, though Rodgers and Hammerstein produced it, and Berlin's score had "There's No Business Like Show Business".
Rodgers and Hammerstein musicals.Kiss Me Kate: It's Cole Porter's work from 1948, and it won the first Tony for Best Musical.
Rodgers and Hammerstein musicals.Cabaret: Kander and Ebb's 1966 musical is set in Berlin in 1931, and is not R&H.
Rodgers and Hammerstein musicals.Gypsy: Styne and Sondheim wrote this 1959 musical about stripper Gypsy Rose Lee and her mother.
Rodgers and Hammerstein musicals.Camelot: Lerner and Loewe's 1960 musical about King Arthur is associated with the Kennedy White House.
Rodgers and Hammerstein musicals.The Music Man: Meredith Willson wrote this 1957 show set in Iowa, and it's not an R&H.
Rodgers and Hammerstein musicals.Brigadoon: Lerner and Loewe's 1947 musical is about a Scottish village that appears for one day every 100 years.
Rodgers and Hammerstein musicals.Mame: Jerry Herman's 1966 hit stars an eccentric aunt, and is not by R&H.
Rodgers and Hammerstein musicals.Funny Girl: Jule Styne wrote it in 1964 for Barbra Streisand, based on Fanny Brice.
Rodgers and Hammerstein musicals.Chicago: Kander and Ebb's 1975 musical was based on 1920s crime reporting, with Bob Fosse choreographing.

Track and field events.Hurdles: Sprinters clear ten barriers per race, and the hurdles tip over, which doesn't count against them, but costs speed.
Track and field events.Long jump: Bob Beamon's 1968 Olympic leap of 8.90 meters beat the record by almost 55 cm and stood for 23 years.
Track and field events.High jump: Dick Fosbury's backward 'Flop' won him the 1968 Olympics, and now nearly every jumper uses it.
Track and field events.Pole vault: Poles were once made of bamboo, then metal, and now fiberglass; the record is over 6 meters, set by Mondo Duplantis.
Track and field events.Shot put: The shot is a heavy metal ball weighing 7.26 kg for men, which is thrown, not actually put, from the shoulder.
Track and field events.Discus: A tricky spin throw, and the discus thrower is among the best-known ancient Greek statues, the Discobolus.
Track and field events.Javelin: The javelin's design was changed in 1986 after throws were getting dangerously far, moving the center of gravity forward.
Track and field events.Hammer throw: The 'hammer' is a metal ball on a wire with a handle; the event grew out of throwing real sledgehammers at old Celtic games.
Track and field events.Triple jump: Athletes hop, step and jump in one sequence; the world record of 18.29 m has stood since 1995 by Jonathan Edwards.
Track and field events.Steeplechase: The 3000 m race includes barriers and a water pit; its name comes from horse races aimed at a church steeple.
Track and field events.Decathlon: Ten events over two days; the winner is often called the world's greatest athlete.
Track and field events.Heptathlon: Seven events for women, which replaced the pentathlon in 1981 and includes 100 m hurdles.
Track and field events.Relay: The 4x100 m is done by passing a baton within a 20 m zone, and dropped batons often cost medals.
Track and field events.Caber toss: A Scottish Highland Games event, tossing a pole that can be 6 meters long; it's not a track and field event.
Track and field events.Butterfly: A swimming stroke, tricky to learn, that was spun off from breaststroke in the 1930s.
Track and field events.Vault: A gymnastics event, not athletics, but the pole vault is a track and field event with a similar name.
Track and field events.Pommel horse: A gymnastics apparatus, where hands move around the handles while the legs swing.
Track and field events.Rings: Suspended gymnastic rings need huge strength, and are in gymnastics, not track and field.
Track and field events.Balance beam: A 10 cm wide beam in gymnastics, not track and field, from which gymnasts perform flips.
Track and field events.Uneven bars: A women's gymnastics event, in which gymnasts swing between two bars set at different heights.
Track and field events.Biathlon: A winter sport combining cross-country skiing and rifle shooting, not track and field.
Track and field events.Moguls: Freestyle skiing over a field of bumps, a winter sport since 1992 at the Olympics.
Track and field events.Halfpipe: A snowboarding and skiing event, with U-shaped snow walls, that Shaun White made famous.
Track and field events.Keirin: A track cycling race, where riders follow a pacer on a motorbike, which began in Japan as betting.

Things on a baseball field.Pitcher's mound: The mound rises 10 inches above the field and stands 60 feet 6 inches from home plate.
Things on a baseball field.Home plate: This five-sided slab has used its pentagon shape since 1900, with the point facing the catcher.
Things on a baseball field.Dugout: Sunk below the field level, it's the covered bench where players wait their turn.
Things on a baseball field.Bullpen: Relief pitchers warm up here, and the origin of the name is still debated by historians.
Things on a baseball field.Infield: The infield diamond measures 90 feet between bases, a distance still unchanged since the 1800s.
Things on a baseball field.Outfield: Unlike in most sports, outfield dimensions vary by park, which is why Boston's Green Monster is unique.
Things on a baseball field.Foul pole: A ball that strikes the pole is fair, which makes it a home run.
Things on a baseball field.Warning track: This dirt strip near the wall lets outfielders know with their feet that the fence is coming up.
Things on a baseball field.Bases: Each base is a 15-inch square, and the bases are padded for safety.
Things on a baseball field.Batter's box: The box measures 4 by 6 feet, and a batter must keep both feet inside it when swinging.
Things on a baseball field.On-deck circle: Next hitters warm up here, swinging weighted bats while the current batter faces the pitcher.
Things on a baseball field.Foul line: A ball touching the line is fair, so the line itself counts as in play.
Things on a baseball field.End zone: It is the scoring zone of American football, 10 yards deep, not part of baseball.
Things on a baseball field.Goalposts: These are the Y-shaped uprights at the back of football's end zone, used for field goals.
Things on a baseball field.Crease: The goalie's marked area in ice hockey, and cricket has a crease too, but baseball does not.
Things on a baseball field.Penalty box: Players serving penalties in hockey sit here, not in a baseball dugout.
Things on a baseball field.Wicket: The cricket target, formed of stumps and bails, has no home on a baseball diamond.
Things on a baseball field.Centre circle: The soccer kickoff mark is not in baseball.
Things on a baseball field.Free-throw line: In basketball it sits 15 feet from the backboard, and free throws begin here.
Things on a baseball field.Bunker: A hazard of sand on a golf course, nothing to do with baseball.
Things on a baseball field.Blue line: Hockey's blue lines divide the ice into zones, and they are painted under the ice.
Things on a baseball field.Fairway: The golf course's mown path between tee and green; baseball has no fairway.
Things on a baseball field.Tee box: Golfers tee off from this box, and baseball players never do.
Things on a baseball field.Six-yard box: Part of the soccer pitch, 6 yards from the goal line, guarded by the keeper.

Video game genres.Platformer: A genre built on jumping between platforms, and it was popularized by Donkey Kong in 1981 and Super Mario Bros. in 1985.
Video game genres.Shooter: A genre focused on aiming and firing, and it dates to 1962's Spacewar! on early computers.
Video game genres.RPG: A role-playing game lets you grow a character through stats and quests, and it grew out of tabletop Dungeons and Dragons.
Video game genres.Puzzle: Games of logic and pattern, and Tetris, created in 1984 by Alexey Pajitnov in Moscow, is the most famous.
Video game genres.Racing: Cars or bikes against the clock or each other, and Gran Turismo and Mario Kart are two of the best-known series.
Video game genres.Sandbox: Open-ended games where players build and explore with few rules, and Minecraft is the best-selling example, at over 300 million copies.
Video game genres.Roguelike: Named after the 1980 game Rogue, these have randomly generated levels and permanent death, so every run is different.
Video game genres.Metroidvania: A mix of Metroid and Castlevania names, it features a large map unlocked by gaining new abilities.
Video game genres.Battle royale: Players fight until one remains in a shrinking arena, and it was inspired by a Japanese novel and film of the same name.
Video game genres.Fighting: One-on-one combat games, and Street Fighter II in 1991 set off an arcade boom.
Video game genres.Rhythm: Players press buttons in time with music, as in Guitar Hero and Dance Dance Revolution.
Video game genres.Stealth: A genre of sneaking past enemies, and Metal Gear and Thief helped establish it.
Video game genres.MMO: Massively multiplayer online games host thousands of players in one world, such as World of Warcraft.
Video game genres.Sitcom: A TV comedy format, and it stands for situation comedy, so it's a TV genre, not a video game one.
Video game genres.Rom-com: A romantic comedy film genre, so it's about movies, not video games.
Video game genres.Documentary: A non-fiction film or TV genre, so it isn't a gaming genre.
Video game genres.Sonnet: A 14-line poem, and Shakespeare wrote 154 of them, none of which is a video game type.
Video game genres.Haiku: A short Japanese poem of 17 syllables in 5-7-5 form, and a poetry form, not a gaming one.
Video game genres.Limerick: A five-line humorous poem, named after a city in Ireland, and not a type of game.
Video game genres.Mockumentary: A fictional film in documentary style like This Is Spinal Tap, and a film genre only.
Video game genres.Opera: A sung stage drama, and a literary form that no game console would call a genre.
Video game genres.Biography: The account of a person's life, a book genre, not a video game genre.
Video game genres.Memoir: A personal written recollection, from the French for memory, and a book genre, not a game one.
Video game genres.Soap opera: Named because early radio serials were sponsored by soap companies, and it's a TV drama genre, not a gaming one.

Invented in the 1800s.Telephone: Alexander Graham Bell patented it in 1876. Elisha Gray filed a similar patent the same day, and a famous dispute followed.
Invented in the 1800s.Light bulb: Edison didn't invent the first one. Joseph Swan and others made earlier versions, but Edison's long-lasting 1879 bulb made it practical.
Invented in the 1800s.Photography: The first permanent photograph was taken by Nicéphore Niépce in the 1820s, needing hours of exposure. Daguerre's process, announced in 1839, made it practical.
Invented in the 1800s.Telegraph: Samuel Morse's electric telegraph went public in 1844 with the message "What hath God wrought". It cut news transmission from weeks to seconds.
Invented in the 1800s.Typewriter: The 1870s Sholes and Glidden machine used the QWERTY layout, popularly said to reduce jams. Mark Twain was an early adopter.
Invented in the 1800s.Dynamite: Alfred Nobel patented it in 1867 to make nitroglycerin safe. His fortune funded the Nobel Prizes.
Invented in the 1800s.Stethoscope: René Laennec invented it in 1816, rolling paper into a tube so he would not need to put his ear to a woman's chest. It was a wooden tube at first.
Invented in the 1800s.Phonograph: Edison's 1877 machine recorded sound on tinfoil cylinders. His first recording was said to be "Mary Had a Little Lamb".
Invented in the 1800s.Sewing machine: Elias Howe patented a lockstitch machine in 1846, and Isaac Singer's later model made sewing machines common in homes.
Invented in the 1800s.Automobile: Karl Benz patented his motorwagen in 1886, with a single-cylinder engine. His wife Bertha made the first long road trip in one in 1888.
Invented in the 1800s.Bicycle: Early 1800s "running machines", with no pedals, led to pedalled models in the 1860s. The "safety bicycle" with a chain emerged in the 1880s.
Invented in the 1800s.Television: The 1920s saw the first working demonstrations, so it belongs to the 20th century. John Logie Baird showed it in 1926.
Invented in the 1800s.Airplane: The Wrights flew on 17 December 1903, which is in the 20th century, not the 19th. Their first flight lasted 12 seconds.
Invented in the 1800s.Internet: It grew from ARPANET in the late 1960s, so a 20th-century creation. The World Wide Web came in 1989.
Invented in the 1800s.Printing press: Johannes Gutenberg's European movable-type press dates to around 1450, centuries earlier than the 1800s.
Invented in the 1800s.Telescope: Appeared in 1608 in the Netherlands, and Galileo turned it on the sky in 1609. It's a 17th-century device.
Invented in the 1800s.Microscope: Arrived around 1600, and Hooke's 1665 Micrographia popularised it. It is much older than the 1800s.
Invented in the 1800s.Gunpowder: From China, several hundred years before the 1800s. It was in use in Europe by the 1300s.
Invented in the 1800s.Microwave oven: Percy Spencer noticed a melted chocolate bar in his pocket near a radar tube in 1945. It's a 20th-century invention.
Invented in the 1800s.Laser: First built in 1960 by Theodore Maiman. Its name stands for light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation.
Invented in the 1800s.Jet engine: Frank Whittle and Hans von Ohain developed it in the 1930s. The first jet flight was in 1939 in Germany.
Invented in the 1800s.Eyeglasses: Invented in northern Italy around the 1280s, some 500 years before the 1800s. They are medieval.
Invented in the 1800s.Smartphone: Appeared in the 1990s, with the iPhone's 2007 launch popularising it. It's a 21st-century everyday object.
Invented in the 1800s.Helicopter: Practical helicopters were built in the 1930s and 40s. Leonardo sketched an air screw in the 1480s.

Famous inventors.Thomas Edison: He held over 1,000 US patents and ran the Menlo Park lab. His practical lightbulb was one of many improvements.
Famous inventors.Nikola Tesla: His alternating-current induction motor shaped the power grid, and the unit of magnetic flux density is named for him.
Famous inventors.Gutenberg: His movable-type press, around 1450 in Mainz, started the age of printing. His Bible ran to roughly 180 copies.
Famous inventors.James Watt: His steam-engine improvements helped drive the Industrial Revolution. He also coined horsepower, and the watt honors him.
Famous inventors.Wright brothers: Bicycle-shop owners who made the first powered flight in 1903. The first lasted only 12 seconds.
Famous inventors.Guglielmo Marconi: He sent wireless signals across the Atlantic in 1901 and won the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Famous inventors.Samuel Morse: A portrait painter before he developed the telegraph. His first long-distance message in 1844 was What hath God wrought.
Famous inventors.Alfred Nobel: The inventor of dynamite left his fortune to found the Nobel Prizes.
Famous inventors.George Eastman: He founded Kodak and made photography simple, with the slogan You press the button, we do the rest.
Famous inventors.Charles Babbage: He designed the Analytical Engine, a programmable mechanical computer, but it was never completed in his lifetime.
Famous inventors.Eli Whitney: His cotton gin of 1793 sped cotton processing, and it increased demand for enslaved labor in the American South.
Famous inventors.Karl Benz: He patented the Motorwagen in 1886, and his wife Bertha made the first long-distance trip in it.
Famous inventors.Louis Braille: Blinded in childhood, he devised his reading system at about age 15, based on a night-writing code for soldiers.
Famous inventors.Shakespeare: A playwright and poet, whose genius was words rather than machines.
Famous inventors.Mozart: A composer who wrote hundreds of works before dying at 35. Music, not machines.
Famous inventors.Napoleon: A general and emperor, with no major inventions. His Napoleonic Code made him a lawgiver.
Famous inventors.Picasso: An artist who co-founded Cubism. He changed how people see, not how machines work.
Famous inventors.Beethoven: A composer who kept writing music as he went deaf. Not an inventor.
Famous inventors.Charles Darwin: A naturalist who proposed evolution by natural selection, a theory rather than an invention.
Famous inventors.Marie Curie: She discovered polonium and radium and won two Nobel Prizes. She is known as a scientist, not as an inventor.
Famous inventors.Sigmund Freud: The founder of psychoanalysis created theories and a therapy, not gadgets.
Famous inventors.Van Gogh: A painter who sold few works in his life. His legacy is art, not inventions.
Famous inventors.Jane Austen: A novelist of Pride and Prejudice, who made characters rather than devices.
Famous inventors.Charles Dickens: A novelist who published his books in serial installments. Not an inventor.

On a Golden Age pirate ship.Cannon: Pirates often fired chain shot to rip rigging and slow a victim, since a prize that stayed afloat was worth far more than a sinking ship.
On a Golden Age pirate ship.Cutlass: The short, curved blade suited crowded decks and tangled rigging, where a long rapier would snag.
On a Golden Age pirate ship.Flintlock pistol: Pirates carried several because each one fired a single shot and took ages to reload in a fight.
On a Golden Age pirate ship.Jolly Roger: Each captain flew his own design, and the black banner was a threat: surrender and live, resist and expect no mercy.
On a Golden Age pirate ship.Rum: Cheap Caribbean sugar rum was everywhere, and it kept pirates cheerful and sometimes dangerously overconfident.
On a Golden Age pirate ship.Spyglass: A brass telescope let lookouts judge a distant sail's nationality and speed long before the other ship saw them.
On a Golden Age pirate ship.Compass: Navigation was a scarce skill, so pirates often seized navigators and charts from captured ships.
On a Golden Age pirate ship.Hammock: Sailors copied this bed from Caribbean peoples whom Columbus's men saw using them, and its sway kept sleepers steady at sea.
On a Golden Age pirate ship.Gunpowder: Some pirate codes banned smoking and lit candles below deck, since a spark near the powder meant disaster.
On a Golden Age pirate ship.Anchor: Pirates often careened ships on quiet beaches, tilting them to scrape off barnacles, held there on anchor.
On a Golden Age pirate ship.Treasure chest: Real pirates rarely buried loot; most cargo was sugar, cloth and tobacco, though Captain Kidd did bury some.
On a Golden Age pirate ship.Hardtack: A rock-hard biscuit that weevils loved; sailors tapped it on the table to knock the bugs out first.
On a Golden Age pirate ship.Radar: Radar was developed in the 1930s, over two centuries after the Golden Age ended around the 1720s.
On a Golden Age pirate ship.Sonar: Sonar came out of the early 1900s, after the Titanic and WWI, not in the age of sail.
On a Golden Age pirate ship.GPS: Satellite navigation arrived in the late 20th century; pirates navigated by stars, compasses and guesswork.
On a Golden Age pirate ship.Outboard motor: Ole Evinrude's first successful outboard dates from about 1909, nearly two centuries too late.
On a Golden Age pirate ship.Steam engine: Steam power reached ships in the early 1800s, long after the Golden Age; pirates relied entirely on wind.
On a Golden Age pirate ship.Radio: Marconi's wireless came in the 1890s; pirates passed news by word of mouth and signal flags.
On a Golden Age pirate ship.Machine gun: Gatling's early gun is from 1861, and Golden Age ships had only cannon and muskets.
On a Golden Age pirate ship.Revolver: Samuel Colt patented his in 1836, about a century after the Golden Age ended.
On a Golden Age pirate ship.Torpedo: Self-propelled torpedoes came in the 1860s, and pirates relied on cannon and boarding.
On a Golden Age pirate ship.Satellite phone: Satellite phones are from the 1990s, so pirates sent word only by passing ships.
On a Golden Age pirate ship.Periscope: Submarine periscopes came in the 1800s and 1900s; pirates just used a lookout in the crow's nest.
On a Golden Age pirate ship.Chainsaw: It was devised for surgery in the 1780s, as a hand-cranked chain saw for childbirth, after the Golden Age ended.

Party supplies.Balloons: Latex balloons float with helium, which is lighter than air, and the gas is also used to cool MRI magnets.
Party supplies.Streamers: Paper streamers date from the 1800s, and the crepe paper they're made from is stretchy because it's crinkled during manufacture.
Party supplies.Party hats: The cone party hat shape became common in the early 1900s, and its elastic chin strap is a more recent addition.
Party supplies.Confetti: Confetti comes from the Italian word for sweets, because it was originally candy and plaster pellets thrown at carnivals.
Party supplies.Paper plates: Paper plates were made in the 1900s, and plastic or wax coatings stop the grease and sauce from soaking through.
Party supplies.Piñata: Piñatas were used in Mexico after missionaries adapted them, though similar candy-filled pots appear in Chinese and European traditions.
Party supplies.Birthday candles: The Germans are often credited with the birthday candle tradition, with a candle for each year plus one for good luck.
Party supplies.Party poppers: A party popper is a small tube with a pull string that triggers a tiny charge, shooting out streamers with a bang.
Party supplies.Banner: A happy birthday banner is often strung on a line, and the word banner goes back to an old word for a military flag.
Party supplies.Noisemakers: Noisemakers have their roots in ancient New Year festivals, where loud sounds were thought to drive off bad spirits.
Party supplies.Goody bags: Goody bags began as a party favor, a small gift for guests, and they now include everything from stickers to sweets.
Party supplies.Stapler: A stapler belongs on the desk, not at the party, and it's a trap, though it does hold up the banner at times.
Party supplies.Toolbox: A toolbox holds hammers and screwdrivers, and it has nothing to do with the party, although it may fix a broken piñata.
Party supplies.Mop: A mop is for cleaning up after the party, not for decorating it.
Party supplies.Plunger: A plunger is for blocked drains, and no party supplies list includes one, unless the party is a very odd one.
Party supplies.Tax forms: Tax forms are a party-killer, and government paperwork would be about as far from fun as a stack of paper could be.
Party supplies.Lawnmower: A lawnmower trims grass before a garden party, but it isn't itself a party supply.
Party supplies.Paint roller: A paint roller coats walls, which is a project, not a party, and it has no place among confetti.
Party supplies.Toilet brush: A toilet brush is a bathroom cleaning tool, which is not what anyone wants to see at a party.
Party supplies.Ironing board: An ironing board is for pressing clothes, and not part of the party kit.
Party supplies.Filing cabinet: A filing cabinet is for storing papers in an office, and there is nothing festive about one.
Party supplies.Snow shovel: A snow shovel moves winter snow, and has no party use, unless the party is outside in a blizzard.
Party supplies.Fire extinguisher: A fire extinguisher is a safety item you hope to keep out of sight at a party, and it isn't a supply.
Party supplies.Mousetrap: A mousetrap catches pests, and a party game called Mouse Trap is a different thing, so it fails on a technicality.

Conditions that affect the heart.Heart attack: A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart is blocked, and women may feel nausea or jaw pain rather than classic chest pain.
Conditions that affect the heart.Arrhythmia: Arrhythmia means an irregular heartbeat, and many cases are harmless, though some need pacemakers or other treatments.
Conditions that affect the heart.Angina: Angina is chest pain from reduced blood flow to the heart muscle, and its name comes from the Latin for a choking pain.
Conditions that affect the heart.Heart murmur: A heart murmur is an extra whooshing sound from blood flow, and many are harmless, especially in children.
Conditions that affect the heart.Cardiac arrest: Cardiac arrest is when the heart suddenly stops pumping, and it is different from a heart attack, which is a blocked artery.
Conditions that affect the heart.Heart failure: Heart failure does not mean the heart has stopped; it means the heart cannot pump as well as the body needs.
Conditions that affect the heart.Atrial fibrillation: Atrial fibrillation, often called AFib, is the most common serious arrhythmia and raises the risk of stroke fivefold.
Conditions that affect the heart.Tachycardia: Tachycardia means a resting heart rate over 100 beats per minute, from the Greek for fast heart.
Conditions that affect the heart.Myocarditis: Myocarditis is inflammation of the heart muscle, usually caused by a viral infection, and it can strike young athletes.
Conditions that affect the heart.Bradycardia: Bradycardia, a slow heartbeat below 60 per minute, can be normal for trained athletes, whose hearts pump more per beat.
Conditions that affect the heart.Heartburn: Heartburn has nothing to do with the heart; it is stomach acid rising into the esophagus, near the heart's location.
Conditions that affect the heart.Asthma: Asthma affects airways in the lungs, not the heart, though shortness of breath can look similar to heart trouble.
Conditions that affect the heart.Migraine: Migraine is a neurological condition, not a heart one, though migraines with aura slightly raise heart risk.
Conditions that affect the heart.Appendicitis: Appendicitis is an inflamed appendix in the lower right abdomen, and it is an issue for the gut, not the heart.
Conditions that affect the heart.Gout: Gout is a painful joint arthritis caused by uric acid crystals, often starting in the big toe.
Conditions that affect the heart.Tonsillitis: Tonsillitis is an infection of the tonsils at the back of the throat, and it does not touch the heart.
Conditions that affect the heart.Hepatitis: Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver, and its name from Greek hepar means liver.
Conditions that affect the heart.Gastritis: Gastritis is stomach lining inflammation, from the Greek gaster for stomach.
Conditions that affect the heart.Bronchitis: Bronchitis inflames the bronchial tubes of the lungs, so it affects breathing and not the heart.
Conditions that affect the heart.Cataract: A cataract is a clouding of the eye's lens, and cataract surgery is among the most common operations worldwide.
Conditions that affect the heart.Scoliosis: Scoliosis is a sideways curve in the spine, and it is a bone issue, not a heart one.
Conditions that affect the heart.Hernia: A hernia is when tissue pushes through a weak spot in a muscle wall, often in the abdomen.
Conditions that affect the heart.Kidney stones: Kidney stones are hard mineral deposits formed in the kidneys, and are often compared with childbirth for pain.
Conditions that affect the heart.Tinnitus: Tinnitus is a ringing in the ears, with no sound source, and it affects about 1 in 10 adults.

Things a classic snowman has.Carrot nose: A carrot's tapered shape makes it the classic snowman nose, and it is also a treat for hungry rabbits, so it may vanish overnight.
Things a classic snowman has.Coal eyes: Lumps of coal were common household fuel when the tradition began, so they were handy for dark eyes. Stones and buttons serve the same job today.
Things a classic snowman has.Scarf: A scarf on the neck is useful for more than looks. Tucked in tightly, it shades the snow from the sun, which can slow melting slightly.
Things a classic snowman has.Top hat: The top hat is a Victorian relic: the tall silk hat marked a gentleman, so dressing a snowman in one made it a very proper figure.
Things a classic snowman has.Buttons: Buttons running down the middle give a snowman a coat. Builders often use coal, stones, or bottle caps, since real ones would get soggy and lost.
Things a classic snowman has.Stick arms: Twigs make the arms, and the best ones are forked so they look like fingers. Snow people have been built with branches for centuries.
Things a classic snowman has.Pipe: The corncob pipe comes from the 1950 song about Frosty the Snowman, which made it part of the look even as modern cartoons often drop it.
Things a classic snowman has.Snowballs: A snowman is stacked snowballs, and it builds best with wet, sticky snow near freezing. Powder snow won't pack and just crumbles apart.
Things a classic snowman has.Coal smile: The smile is usually an arc of small pieces of coal or stones. Snowmen are among the earliest known winter art, with medieval records of them in Europe.
Things a classic snowman has.Flip-flops: Flip-flops are for sand and sun. A snowman has no feet to wear them, and the whole idea is the opposite of a frozen figure.
Things a classic snowman has.Sunscreen: Fresh snow reflects up to about 80 percent of UV rays, so skiers need sunscreen. A snowman, though, wants shade and cold, not protection from tanning.
Things a classic snowman has.Hair dryer: A hair dryer blows hot air for drying hair, which would turn a snowman into a puddle. It's a natural enemy of anything frozen.
Things a classic snowman has.Swimsuit: A swimsuit belongs by the water, and water is a snowman's greatest enemy: it melts him. No swim lessons for the frozen.
Things a classic snowman has.Heat lamp: A heat lamp radiates infrared warmth for keeping food or people warm. Pointed at a snowman, it would melt him in minutes.
Things a classic snowman has.Space heater: A space heater warms a room with hot coils, and a snowman cannot survive indoors. It is exactly what he must avoid.
Things a classic snowman has.Bonfire: A bonfire lights up a winter night and warms people nearby, but standing close would melt a snowman into a puddle.
Things a classic snowman has.Toaster: Toaster coils reach several hundred degrees Celsius. It is a kitchen appliance that would be bad news for any snowman.
Things a classic snowman has.Beach towel: A beach towel dries swimmers on a sunny shore. A snowman wants to stay frozen and dry, so it is out of place.
Things a classic snowman has.Lawnmower: A lawnmower is a summer tool. Snow cover and grass mowing don't share a season, which is why the two never meet.
Things a classic snowman has.Blowtorch: A blowtorch flame reaches over a thousand degrees Celsius, which would vaporize a snowman in seconds. It is no part of building one.
Things a classic snowman has.Laptop: A laptop is an indoor, electric item that cold and wet conditions can damage. It does not belong in a snowman's classic outfit.
Things a classic snowman has.Sneakers: Sneakers are shoes, but a snowman is just a stack of snowballs with no legs or feet, so he has nothing to put them on.
Things a classic snowman has.Backpack: A backpack is for hikers and students on the move. A snowman stays rooted to one spot and has nothing to carry.
Things a classic snowman has.Necktie: A necktie is office wear and doesn't match the winter look. A snowman's neck dress is a woolly scarf, not a tie.

Things you'd hate to sit on.Wet paint: Wet paint is a classic sitting hazard, and that's why 'wet paint' signs are one of the most recognized warning signs.
Things you'd hate to sit on.Chewing gum: Chewing gum under a seat is a nuisance to cities, and cleaning it up costs places like London millions every year.
Things you'd hate to sit on.Hot stove: A hot stove burns in seconds, and skin damage starts at around 50 C, well below a stovetop's temperature.
Things you'd hate to sit on.Whoopee cushion: The whoopee cushion's rude noise made it a prank classic since the 1920s, and it was supposedly invented by a Canadian rubber company.
Things you'd hate to sit on.Ant hill: An ant hill can hold hundreds of thousands of ants, and some species, such as fire ants, bite and sting hard.
Things you'd hate to sit on.Stinging nettles: Stinging nettles carry tiny hairs that inject chemicals, which explains the burn, though cooked nettles make a good soup.
Things you'd hate to sit on.Melted chocolate: Melted chocolate on a seat is a messy nightmare, and chocolate melts just below body temperature, which is why it melts in your mouth.
Things you'd hate to sit on.Puddle: A puddle is a soggy surprise, and the word 'puddle' is old, but water on a seat will soak through fast.
Things you'd hate to sit on.Cream pie: A cream pie is a slapstick staple, and pie throwing in comedy goes back to silent films of the 1910s.
Things you'd hate to sit on.Birthday cake: A birthday cake under you would be an unhappy surprise, and the candle-and-cake tradition dates to ancient Greece.
Things you'd hate to sit on.Hot grill: A hot grill can top 250 C, which is more than enough to burn through a swimsuit, so sit on it only in dreams.
Things you'd hate to sit on.Wasp: A wasp can sting repeatedly, unlike honeybees, which usually lose their stinger and die after one sting.
Things you'd hate to sit on.Your own glasses: Sitting on your own glasses is a real classic accident, and frames and lenses crack easily when sat on in a pocket.
Things you'd hate to sit on.Armchair: An armchair fits what you'd happily sit in, and the French call a classic one a 'bergere', a name for a comfy chair.
Things you'd hate to sit on.Sofa: Sofa comes from an Arabic word, 'suffa', meaning a bench, and early European sofas were a luxury of the wealthy.
Things you'd hate to sit on.Stool: A stool is the simplest seat, and stools predate chairs by thousands of years, appearing in ancient Egypt.
Things you'd hate to sit on.Beanbag: The beanbag chair was invented in Italy in 1968, called 'Sacco', and it was a hit for its shape-molding comfort.
Things you'd hate to sit on.Cushion: Cushions are padded for comfort, and the word comes from an old French word, 'coussin', meaning pillow.
Things you'd hate to sit on.Throne: The throne is a symbolic seat of power, and the Iron Throne of fiction sits in a world with swords for its legs.
Things you'd hate to sit on.Saddle: A saddle is a seat designed for riding, and the earliest known stirrups came centuries after the first saddles.
Things you'd hate to sit on.Swing: A swing is a seat on ropes, and playground swings are made with soft seats because hard ones hit harder.
Things you'd hate to sit on.Park bench: A park bench is a public seat, and benches are often donated by families with a little plaque in memory of a loved one.
Things you'd hate to sit on.Picnic blanket: A picnic blanket is a seat on the ground, and the word 'picnic' comes from French, referring to a meal with shared contributions.
Things you'd hate to sit on.Rocking chair: A rocking chair has curved runners, and Benjamin Franklin is often credited with it, although this is not certain.

Things you should never shake.Soda can: A shaken soda can sprays when opened because the jostling forms bubbles that push the liquid out.
Things you should never shake.Hornet nest: Hornets defend their nests aggressively; shaking one means a swarm of stinging, venom-injecting insects coming for you.
Things you should never shake.Beehive: Shaking a beehive angers thousands of bees at once, and some honey bees will chase an intruder a long way.
Things you should never shake.Sleeping bear: Disturbing a sleeping bear is a terrible idea; bears in hibernation can wake up fast and are very defensive.
Things you should never shake.Vending machine: Vending machines weigh hundreds of kilos, and tipping them over while shaking has killed a number of people.
Things you should never shake.Champagne bottle: A shaken champagne bottle has pressure of about 6 atmospheres, and the cork can fly at roughly 40 mph.
Things you should never shake.Bowl of soup: Shaking a bowl of soup is a quick way to wear it; hot liquids burn, and it ends with the floor wet.
Things you should never shake.Full coffee cup: A full coffee cup shaken spills, and the liquid is hot enough to scald; spills are a leading cause of mug burns.
Things you should never shake.Fish tank: Shaking a fish tank stresses the fish and can crack the glass or send water everywhere, which can wreck a floor.
Things you should never shake.House of cards: A house of cards depends on friction and balance, and even a tiny shake can bring the whole structure down.
Things you should never shake.Snow globe: A trap: a snow globe is made to be shaken, which is the whole fun; it makes flakes swirl down.
Things you should never shake.Maracas: Maracas are shaken to play them; they're traditional in Latin American music and often filled with seeds.
Things you should never shake.Salt shaker: A salt shaker is shaken by design; a few grains of rice can keep it from clumping in humid weather.
Things you should never shake.Ketchup bottle: Ketchup bottles are meant to be shaken; the sauce gets thinner when stressed, which is why it pours so suddenly.
Things you should never shake.Protein shake: A protein shake needs shaking, since the powder settles and clumps without being mixed.
Things you should never shake.Paint can: Paint cans should be stirred or shaken to mix the pigments that settle at the bottom.
Things you should never shake.Dice: Dice are shaken before a throw, and the practice is thousands of years old; ancient dice were made from bones.
Things you should never shake.Tambourine: A tambourine is shaken to play it, and the metal jingles are called zils.
Things you should never shake.Magic 8 Ball: A Magic 8 Ball is made to be shaken; inside, a floating die with answers rises to a window.
Things you should never shake.Etch A Sketch: The Etch A Sketch is shaken to erase the drawing, as the aluminium powder inside coats the screen again.
Things you should never shake.Spray paint can: Spray paint cans contain a small ball, and you hear it rattle; shaking mixes the paint and propellant.
Things you should never shake.Cocktail shaker: A cocktail shaker is meant to be shaken; the shaking chills the drink quickly and adds tiny air bubbles.
Things you should never shake.Rattle: A baby rattle is designed to be shaken; babies learn cause and effect by shaking them.
Things you should never shake.Salad dressing: Salad dressing separates into oil and vinegar, and shaking the bottle emulsifies them temporarily.

Things you'd find on a résumé.Work experience: Usually listed with the most recent job first, since recruiters often give a résumé only a few seconds on a first look.
Things you'd find on a résumé.Education: Degrees and schools are listed here, and for recent graduates the education usually goes at the top.
Things you'd find on a résumé.Skills: Skills lists are mostly searched by software, since many companies use tracking systems that filter résumés by keywords.
Things you'd find on a résumé.References: Many résumés now say "available on request" instead of listing referees, saving space for more useful content.
Things you'd find on a résumé.Contact details: An email and phone number are essential, and in some countries a résumé also includes a photo, though not in the US.
Things you'd find on a résumé.Objective: An objective statement is a one-line goal at the top, and many career experts now suggest a short summary instead.
Things you'd find on a résumé.Certifications: Certifications show proven training, such as first aid, project management or a language exam, and can stand out as proof.
Things you'd find on a résumé.Languages: Listing languages is useful, and it's wise to say your level, such as fluent, conversational or basic.
Things you'd find on a résumé.Awards: Awards show recognition, and employers like numbers or context behind them, such as "top 5% of the team."
Things you'd find on a résumé.Volunteer work: Volunteer experience counts as real experience and can fill a gap or show skills that paid jobs haven't.
Things you'd find on a résumé.Blood type: Blood type is private medical information with no bearing on a job, so a résumé never needs it.
Things you'd find on a résumé.Shoe size: Unless you apply as a model or a shoe tester, nobody needs this, and the number never shows up on a résumé.
Things you'd find on a résumé.Star sign: Employers don't use astrology, and in many places asking about it would be considered irrelevant to hiring.
Things you'd find on a résumé.Credit card number: Never put this on a résumé; résumés get passed around and a credit card number is an invitation to fraud.
Things you'd find on a résumé.Password: Passwords are secret, and a résumé is meant to be shared, so putting one down would be risky.
Things you'd find on a résumé.Bank PIN: A PIN is secret and one reason a résumé must never contain private codes.
Things you'd find on a résumé.Body weight: In many countries it's illegal to ask for this, and a résumé needn't have any physical measurements.
Things you'd find on a résumé.Medical history: Health details are private, and in many places employers cannot require them before an offer.
Things you'd find on a résumé.Pet's name: A pet's name is a common password hint, so it's a bad detail for a public résumé.
Things you'd find on a résumé.Favorite cereal: Charming, but irrelevant to hiring, though a personal touch can sometimes humanize a cover letter.
This number is the key to identity theft, and a résumé should never include it.
Things you'd find on a résumé.Childhood nickname: A nickname from childhood rarely helps, and a résumé needs your professional name.
Things you'd find on a résumé.Diary entries: Diaries are private, and a résumé should be a polished document, not a personal journal.
Things you'd find on a résumé.Grocery list: A grocery list is for the supermarket, not a hiring manager, even if it shows organization.

Things a janitor uses.Mop: Thomas W. Stewart, a Black inventor, patented a self-wringing mop in 1893, sparing cleaners from wringing dirty water by hand.
Things a janitor uses.Bucket: A rolling mop bucket with a built-in wringer lets one person clean a whole corridor without much bending or lifting.
Things a janitor uses.Broom: Brooms were once made from the broom plant, a shrub with bendy twigs, and that is where the tool got its name.
Things a janitor uses.Vacuum cleaner: Hubert Booth's 1901 vacuum was a horse-drawn machine parked outside, with hoses fed through windows to suck dust from the rooms.
Things a janitor uses.Dustpan: Its thin front edge lies flat on the floor, so the broom can sweep dirt straight onto it with no lip to catch on.
Things a janitor uses.Floor buffer: A heavy rotating machine that spins abrasive pads over a floor, grinding away scuffs and leaving a gleaming polish.
Things a janitor uses.Bleach: Never mix it with ammonia-based cleaners, since the two make a toxic gas, a classic cleaning accident worth knowing.
Things a janitor uses.Trash bags: Harry Wasylyk and Larry Hansen invented the plastic garbage bag in Canada in the 1950s, first for use in hospitals and homes.
Things a janitor uses.Rubber gloves: Rubber surgical gloves were first made around 1889 for nurse Caroline Hampton, whose hands were irritated by disinfectant.
Things a janitor uses.Toilet brush: Ancient Romans used a communal sponge on a stick, called a tersorium, for the same job, rinsed in vinegar water or salt water.
Things a janitor uses.Wet floor sign: Slips and falls are among the leading workplace injuries, which is why that bright yellow warning sign matters so much.
Things a janitor uses.Scalpel: A surgeon's blade is among the sharpest tools anywhere, with a razor edge that is replaced after each operation.
Things a janitor uses.Easel: An artist's stand that holds a canvas upright, and nothing about it helps a janitor clean a floor.
Things a janitor uses.Stethoscope: A doctor's listening device, invented in 1816, used to hear the heart and lungs rather than to clean up.
Things a janitor uses.Gavel: A judge's mallet used to call for order in court, and not something a janitor keeps in the cleaning closet.
Things a janitor uses.Telescope: Galileo turned a telescope on Jupiter in 1610 and found its four largest moons, but it would be useless for sweeping.
Things a janitor uses.Saddle: A riding seat for horses, which a janitor never needs, though a rolling mop bucket does have wheels.
Things a janitor uses.Anvil: A blacksmith's heavy block of steel, often weighing over 100 pounds, made for hammering hot metal rather than mopping.
Things a janitor uses.Lasso: A rope loop used to catch cattle, and the word comes from the Spanish for a snare, so it does not help in a school.
Things a janitor uses.Harpoon: A barbed spear tied to a line, used on whales and big fish, and certainly not a tool for cleaning a hallway.
Things a janitor uses.Sextant: A navigation tool for measuring the angle of a star above the horizon, from the days before GPS satellites.
Things a janitor uses.Microscope: A lab instrument for seeing tiny things, such as the germs and dust mites a janitor tries to clean away.
Things a janitor uses.Baton: A conductor's stick; the composer Lully died in 1687 after stabbing his own foot with his heavy conducting staff.
Things a janitor uses.Pitchfork: A long-handled farm tool with sharp tines for lifting hay, and entirely out of place in a school hallway or office.

Things in a factory.Assembly line: Henry Ford's plant adopted the moving assembly line in 1913, cutting Model T chassis assembly from about 12 hours to roughly 1.5 hours.
Things in a factory.Conveyor belt: Conveyor belts keep products moving between stations at a steady pace, the same idea that carries luggage at airports.
Things in a factory.Forklift: Forklifts steer with their rear wheels, which lets them turn in very tight warehouse aisles.
Things in a factory.Time clock: Time clocks recorded when each worker arrived. The first ones, from the 1880s, punched holes in a card.
Things in a factory.Robot arm: The first industrial robot, Unimate, started work on a General Motors line in 1961, lifting hot metal parts.
Things in a factory.Loading dock: Loading docks sit at truck-bed height so goods can roll straight on and off trucks without any lifting.
Things in a factory.Hard hats: The modern hard hat dates to about 1919, when a company made one from steam-treated canvas and glue after seeing miners' hats.
Things in a factory.Pallets: Standard pallets let a forklift lift a whole stack of goods at once, and global trade relies on a handful of standard sizes.
Things in a factory.Control panel: A control panel puts a machine's buttons, dials and emergency stop in one place, so an operator can manage a whole process.
Things in a factory.Safety signs: Safety signs use color codes: red means stop or danger, yellow means caution, and green marks safe exits and first aid.
Things in a factory.Machinery: The earliest mechanized factories, such as English cotton mills, were powered by water long before steam or electricity.
Things in a factory.Overalls: Overalls keep clothing from catching in moving machinery, one reason loose sleeves and dangling items are banned on factory floors.
Things in a factory.Altar: An altar is a table for religious rites, found in churches and temples, not on a factory floor.
Things in a factory.Pulpit: A pulpit is the raised stand a preacher speaks from. A factory floor has a supervisor's platform at best, with no sermons.
Things in a factory.Jury box: A jury box seats the jurors in a courtroom. Factories need quality inspectors, not verdicts.
Things in a factory.Hot tub: A hot tub is a heated bubbling pool for relaxing, which is the opposite of what a busy production floor is for.
Things in a factory.Ball pit: A ball pit is for children's play areas. Factories do sometimes have ball bearings, which is a different thing.
Things in a factory.Dental chair: A dental chair reclines under a bright lamp in a dentist's office. A production line has stools and workstations.
Things in a factory.Barber's chair: A barber's chair pumps up and down for haircuts. Factories have workbenches, not styling stations.
Things in a factory.Hymn books: Hymn books are sung from in church services. Factories occasionally have music, but through speakers, not songbooks.
Things in a factory.Chandelier: A chandelier is a decorative lit fixture for grand halls. Factories use plain, bright, functional lights.
Things in a factory.Four-poster bed: A four-poster bed is a fancy bedroom piece with tall posts, nothing like a bunk in a factory dorm.
Things in a factory.Bathtub: A bathtub belongs in a bathroom. Factories have washing stations for workers, but not baths.
Things in a factory.Jukebox: A jukebox plays records in a diner or bar. Factory floors do sometimes play music, but through speakers.

Things you'll find in an email app.Inbox: Google also ran a separate app called Inbox from 2014 to 2019 before folding its ideas back into Gmail.
Things you'll find in an email app.Outbox: A message only sits here until it can be sent, so you see it mostly when you're offline.
Things you'll find in an email app.Drafts: Gmail autosaves as you type, so a half-written note is usually safe even if the tab crashes.
Things you'll find in an email app.Spam folder: Named after the canned meat via a Monty Python sketch in which the word is repeated endlessly.
Things you'll find in an email app.Sent folder: Keeps copies of everything you send, which can serve as proof of what you wrote and when.
Things you'll find in an email app.Reply all: The button behind many notorious office email storms, where one reply floods thousands of inboxes.
Things you'll find in an email app.CC: Short for carbon copy, from the days when typists slipped carbon paper between sheets.
Things you'll find in an email app.BCC: Blind carbon copy hides recipients from one another, so you can email a group without exposing addresses.
Things you'll find in an email app.Attachment: Early email was text-only; the MIME standard of the 1990s made attachments practical.
Things you'll find in an email app.Subject line: Mobile apps cut off long ones, so it pays to put the key words first.
Things you'll find in an email app.Signature: Auto-added sign-off, and the line 'Sent from my iPhone' became a famous excuse for typos.
Things you'll find in an email app.Hashtag: Chris Messina proposed using # on Twitter in 2007; it belongs to social media, not email.
Things you'll find in an email app.Retweet: A Twitter feature; the platform, now called X, has since renamed it a repost.
Things you'll find in an email app.Story: Snapchat introduced these in 2013, and Instagram copied the idea in 2016.
Things you'll find in an email app.Reel: An Instagram video format launched in 2020 as a TikTok competitor.
Things you'll find in an email app.Playlist: A music-app feature, though email has folders instead.
Things you'll find in an email app.Subscriber: A tricky one: email newsletters have subscribers, but the email app itself does not.
Things you'll find in an email app.Like button: Facebook's Like button launched in 2009; it was nearly named the Awesome button.
Things you'll find in an email app.Follower: A social-media feature, not an email one.
Things you'll find in an email app.Swipe right: Tinder popularized the gesture in 2012; email apps use swiping for archiving.
Things you'll find in an email app.Livestream: A real-time video feature; email can't broadcast.
Things you'll find in an email app.Duet: A TikTok feature that places your video next to someone else's.
Things you'll find in an email app.Upvote: A Reddit feature, where posts rise or sink by votes.
Things you'll find in an email app.Stitch: A TikTok feature letting you clip part of another video into your own.

Parts found on a circuit board.Resistor: Limits current flow, and the colored stripes on it are a code for its value.
Parts found on a circuit board.Capacitor: Stores charge briefly, and camera flashes use big ones to release a sudden burst.
Parts found on a circuit board.Transistor: Invented at Bell Labs in 1947, it's the switch behind all digital logic, and modern chips hold billions.
Parts found on a circuit board.Diode: Lets current flow in one direction only, working as a one-way valve for electricity.
Parts found on a circuit board.LED: A light-emitting diode; the blue LED took until the 1990s to invent and won a 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Parts found on a circuit board.Microchip: A tiny slice of silicon packed with transistors; Jack Kilby demonstrated the first integrated circuit in 1958.
Parts found on a circuit board.Solder: A tin-based alloy melted to join parts, with lead-free versions now standard because of environmental rules.
Parts found on a circuit board.Inductor: A coil that stores energy in a magnetic field and resists changes in current.
Parts found on a circuit board.Crystal oscillator: A vibrating quartz crystal that acts as the board's clock, just like in quartz watches.
Parts found on a circuit board.Copper trace: Thin copper lines etched on the board work as its wires, and designers widen them to carry more current.
Parts found on a circuit board.Pixel: A trap: a pixel is a picture element on a screen, a display concept, not a component.
