Parts found on a circuit board.Cursor: The on-screen pointer is software, not a part you can solder.
Parts found on a circuit board.Cookie: A small text file saved by websites; the name probably comes from the Unix term magic cookie.
Parts found on a circuit board.Firewall: The name comes from fire-resistant walls in buildings. This one is a security concept, not a board part.
Parts found on a circuit board.Hashtag: A hashtag is a # symbol and a tag; the Twitter-era use was proposed by Chris Messina in 2007.
Parts found on a circuit board.Browser: Software for viewing websites; Mosaic and Netscape started the browser era in the 1990s.
Parts found on a circuit board.Spreadsheet: Software; VisiCalc in 1979 was the killer app that helped sell the Apple II.
Parts found on a circuit board.Folder: A software metaphor borrowed from office filing, not something soldered onto a board.
Parts found on a circuit board.Desktop: A screen metaphor from Xerox PARC research; the computer itself may be a desktop, but it's not a part on a board.
Parts found on a circuit board.Wallpaper: The name borrows from decorative paper on walls; it's a software setting unrelated to the board.
Parts found on a circuit board.Emoji: Japanese for picture character, unrelated to the word emotion; Shigetaka Kurita designed the first set in 1999.
Parts found on a circuit board.Avatar: A Sanskrit word for a deity's descent to earth, which became a term for your online figure.
Parts found on a circuit board.Bookmark: A saved link in your browser; the word is borrowed from paper books, and it's a software feature, not hardware.
Parts found on a circuit board.Tab: A browser and interface feature, so it's not a board part. The Tab key is on the keyboard, a different thing.

Poetic forms.Sonnet: Fourteen lines of tightly argued verse; Shakespeare wrote 154 of them and made the form famous.
Poetic forms.Haiku: Traditionally 5-7-5 and anchored by a seasonal word. Japanese haiku actually count sound units, which are shorter than English syllables.
Poetic forms.Limerick: Edward Lear made the five-line comic form famous, and the name probably honors Limerick, Ireland.
Poetic forms.Ode: Originally sung to music in ancient Greece, an ode praises its subject; Keats wrote one to a nightingale.
Poetic forms.Elegy: A poem of mourning; Thomas Gray's 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard' is one of the best-known in English.
Poetic forms.Villanelle: Nineteen lines with two repeating refrains; Dylan Thomas used it for 'Do not go gentle into that good night.'
Poetic forms.Ballad: A story told in song-like verse, often in four-line stanzas; folk ones circulated orally for centuries before being written down.
Poetic forms.Sestina: Thirty-nine lines in which the same six end-words rotate in a set pattern, a form credited to the troubadour Arnaut Daniel.
Poetic forms.Tanka: An older Japanese cousin of haiku, with five lines of roughly 31 syllables, often about love or loss.
Poetic forms.Ghazal: Rhyming couplets with a refrain, from Arabic, Persian and Urdu poetry; Rumi and Hafez wrote them.
Poetic forms.Free verse: Verse without a set rhythm or rhyme; Robert Frost quipped that writing it was like playing tennis with the net down.
Poetic forms.Acrostic: The first letters of lines spell a word. Lewis Carroll ended Through the Looking-Glass with one spelling Alice Liddell's name.
Poetic forms.Cinquain: Five lines in a 2-4-6-8-2 syllable pattern, invented by the American poet Adelaide Crapsey.
Poetic forms.Novella: A prose work longer than a short story but shorter than a novel, such as Of Mice and Men.
Poetic forms.Essay: Prose, not verse: Montaigne coined the form, from French 'essai', meaning an attempt, and his 16th-century musings still read freshly.
Poetic forms.Memoir: A prose account of the author's own life and memories, written by the person themselves, unlike a biography, which is written by someone else.
Poetic forms.Biography: Prose about a person's life; Boswell's Life of Samuel Johnson is a famous early example.
Poetic forms.Thesis: A prose paper defending a claim, from the Greek for 'a placing'; a doctoral candidate defends one, but no one has to rhyme.
Poetic forms.Anecdote: A short true story; the Greek word 'anekdota' meant 'unpublished things', after Procopius's secret history.
Poetic forms.Novel: A long prose narrative, not verse; many scholars call Cervantes's 1605 Don Quixote the first modern novel.
Poetic forms.Screenplay: A script for film or TV, not a poem; the usual rule of thumb is that one formatted page equals about a minute of screen time.
Poetic forms.Short story: A brief prose tale meant to be read in one sitting; Edgar Allan Poe argued it should create a single effect on the reader.
Poetic forms.Op-ed: It means 'opposite the editorial page', where these pieces once appeared, not 'opinion-editorial'.
Poetic forms.Obituary: A death notice in prose; newspapers often write them for famous people long before they die.

Venues for opera or ballet.La Scala: Milan's opera house opened in 1778, and its season traditionally begins each December 7, the feast of Saint Ambrose.
Venues for opera or ballet.Bolshoi Theatre: Moscow's theatre, whose name means "big", staged the premiere of Swan Lake in 1877.
Venues for opera or ballet.Sydney Opera House: Jørn Utzon's sail-roofed building took 14 years to finish and opened in 1973; it is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Venues for opera or ballet.Palais Garnier: This Paris opera house, with a lake underground, inspired the setting of The Phantom of the Opera.
Venues for opera or ballet.Royal Opera House: Covent Garden's theatre is the third on its site, because two earlier buildings burned down.
Venues for opera or ballet.Metropolitan Opera: The Saturday radio broadcasts from this New York house began in 1931, making them among radio's longest-running shows.
Venues for opera or ballet.Vienna State Opera: Vienna's opera house opened in 1869 and each year turns into a ballroom for the Vienna Opera Ball.
Venues for opera or ballet.Teatro Colón: Buenos Aires's opera house, opened in 1908, is rated among the world's best for acoustics.
Venues for opera or ballet.La Fenice: Venice's opera house, whose name means "the phoenix", burned down in 1996 and was rebuilt, reopening in 2003.
Venues for opera or ballet.Mariinsky Theatre: Saint Petersburg's theatre staged Tchaikovsky's Nutcracker and Sleeping Beauty premieres.
Venues for opera or ballet.Kennedy Center: Washington's performing arts center is a living memorial to President Kennedy and opened in 1971.
Venues for opera or ballet.Lincoln Center: New York's arts complex houses the Met Opera and New York City Ballet; it replaced the crowded San Juan Hill neighborhood.
Venues for opera or ballet.Louvre: Paris's great art museum is for paintings and statues; opera isn't performed here, though it was once a palace.
Venues for opera or ballet.Uffizi: Florence's museum is for Renaissance art, in a building the Medici built as offices.
Venues for opera or ballet.Prado: Madrid's museum is devoted to paintings by Velázquez, Goya and El Greco, not performances.
Venues for opera or ballet.Tate Modern: London's modern art museum is in a power station; no opera or ballet is staged here.
Venues for opera or ballet.MoMA: New York's museum of modern art holds paintings and a Starry Night, not staged shows.
Venues for opera or ballet.Guggenheim: The spiral museum in New York is for art, designed by Frank Lloyd Wright.
Venues for opera or ballet.Rijksmuseum: Amsterdam's art museum exhibits Rembrandt, not ballet.
Venues for opera or ballet.Musée d'Orsay: Paris's old railway station is a museum of Impressionist art, not a stage.
Venues for opera or ballet.Getty Center: Los Angeles's hilltop art complex is a museum and gardens, not an opera house.
Venues for opera or ballet.British Museum: London's museum, founded in 1753, holds the Rosetta Stone and is for artifacts, not performances.
Venues for opera or ballet.Colosseum: Rome's amphitheater hosted gladiator fights, not opera or ballet, though it is a famous ancient venue.
Venues for opera or ballet.Wembley Stadium: England's national football stadium, with a famous arch, hosts concerts and matches, not opera or ballet.

Irish writers.James Joyce: Ulysses unfolds on a single day, 16 June 1904, which Dublin and fans worldwide celebrate each year as Bloomsday.
Irish writers.Oscar Wilde: Wilde wrote only one novel, The Picture of Dorian Gray, and served two years' hard labor before dying in Paris in 1900.
Irish writers.W. B. Yeats: Yeats won the Nobel Prize in 1923 and also served as a senator in the new Irish Free State.
Irish writers.Samuel Beckett: Beckett wrote Waiting for Godot first in French, then translated it himself, and won the Nobel Prize in 1969.
Irish writers.Bram Stoker: Dracula's creator managed Henry Irving's Lyceum Theatre in London, and the novel sold only modestly during his life.
Irish writers.Jonathan Swift: The Dean of St Patrick's Cathedral wrote Gulliver's Travels and also A Modest Proposal, which satirically suggests eating poor children.
Irish writers.Seamus Heaney: The Nobel winner of 1995 began his career with poems about digging peat and potatoes, such as 'Digging'.
Irish writers.George Bernard Shaw: He is the only person to win both a Nobel Prize in Literature (1925) and an Oscar, for the screenplay of Pygmalion.
Irish writers.Sally Rooney: Her novel Normal People became a hit 2020 TV series, and she was only in her twenties when her debut appeared.
Irish writers.Roddy Doyle: His Barrytown novels, such as The Commitments, were followed by a 1993 Booker Prize for Paddy Clarke Ha Ha Ha.
Irish writers.Edna O'Brien: Her 1960 debut The Country Girls was banned in Ireland for its frank view of women's lives.
Irish writers.Oliver Goldsmith: An 18th-century Irishman who wrote the novel The Vicar of Wakefield and the comedy She Stoops to Conquer.
Irish writers.Robert Burns: Scotland's national poet, who wrote Auld Lang Syne, is honored on Burns Night each 25 January, so he's Scottish, not Irish.
Irish writers.Walter Scott: The Scottish novelist of Ivanhoe and Rob Roy has Edinburgh's Waverley station named after his novels, so he isn't Irish.
Irish writers.R. L. Stevenson: The Scottish author of Treasure Island died in Samoa, where locals called him Tusitala, the 'teller of tales'.
Irish writers.Arthur Conan Doyle: He was born in Edinburgh, so Scottish by birth, though his family was of Irish Catholic descent, which makes him a tempting trap.
Irish writers.J. M. Barrie: The creator of Peter Pan was born in Kirriemuir, Scotland, so he belongs on the Scottish list, not the Irish one.
Irish writers.Dylan Thomas: The Welsh poet of Under Milk Wood and 'Do not go gentle into that good night' came from Swansea, not Ireland.
Irish writers.Roald Dahl: Roald Dahl was born in Cardiff, Wales, to Norwegian parents, and gave the world Matilda and the BFG, not Ireland.
Irish writers.Charles Dickens: Dickens was English, born in Portsmouth, and set most of his novels in London, though he gave reading tours in Ireland.
Irish writers.Thomas Hardy: Thomas Hardy set his novels in a fictional Wessex based on his native Dorset, so he is English, not Irish.
Irish writers.Rudyard Kipling: Kipling was English, though born in Bombay; in 1907 he became the first English-language writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.
Irish writers.Agatha Christie: Agatha Christie was born in Torquay, Devon, and became the best-selling novelist of all time; she's English, not Irish.
Irish writers.Jane Austen: Jane Austen lived in Hampshire and Bath, in England, and wrote six finished novels, so she isn't on the Irish list.

Transparent things.Window pane: Glass is transparent because its atoms don't absorb visible light, so photons pass straight through.
Transparent things.Cling film: Thin plastic wrap is a clear polymer, and one version, polyvinylidene chloride, was discovered by accident in a lab in 1933.
Transparent things.Tap water: Pure water is transparent, and sunlight can penetrate clear ocean water to about 200 meters.
Transparent things.Air: Air is transparent, so you only see the sky because it scatters blue light.
Transparent things.Contact lens: The earliest contact lenses were made of glass in 1887, and modern soft ones are mostly water.
Transparent things.Eyeglass lens: Lenses are clear to let light through, and the first eyeglasses were made in Italy in the 1280s.
Transparent things.Windshield: A car windshield is laminated glass with a plastic layer, which is why it cracks and holds together.
Transparent things.Magnifying glass: Magnifying lenses are curved to bend light into focus, and can set paper on fire in sunlight.
Transparent things.Diamond: A pure diamond is transparent, and its high refractive index gives it its sparkle.
Transparent things.Fish tank: An aquarium works because water and glass are transparent, and fish can see out too.
Transparent things.Glass of water: Water in a glass is see-through, although a full glass bends light and flips the image behind it.
Transparent things.Frosted glass: Frosted glass is translucent: its rough surface scatters light so shapes blur, but light gets through.
Transparent things.Wax paper: Wax paper lets light through but scatters it, so you can see shapes but not details, making it translucent.
Transparent things.Milk: Milk is opaque because fat and protein droplets scatter light in all directions.
Transparent things.Mirror: A mirror has a metal backing that reflects light, so you can't see through it.
Transparent things.Brick: Brick is fired clay, which is dense and opaque, so it blocks all light and offers no view through it.
Transparent things.Cardboard: Cardboard blocks light, so it is opaque.
Transparent things.Aluminum foil: Aluminum foil reflects light, and even a thin sheet blocks it.
Transparent things.Smoke: Smoke is made of particles that scatter light, so it is not transparent.
Transparent things.Fog: Fog is billions of tiny water droplets that scatter light, so it blurs and blocks vision.
Transparent things.Coffee: Black coffee absorbs most visible light, and it's opaque in a mug.
Transparent things.Wood: Wood is opaque, though very thin slices of wood veneer can let light through.
Transparent things.Tissue paper: Tissue paper is translucent: light passes through, but images don't.
Transparent things.Orange juice: OJ is cloudy with pulp that scatters light, which makes it opaque.

Real spacecraft, not fictional ones.Sputnik: Sputnik 1, launched in 1957, was about the size of a beach ball and beeped radio signals that amateurs around the world tracked.
Real spacecraft, not fictional ones.Voyager 1: Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object and entered interstellar space in 2012.
Real spacecraft, not fictional ones.Space Shuttle: The Space Shuttle flew 135 missions between 1981 and 2011, and two orbiters, Challenger and Columbia, were lost.
Real spacecraft, not fictional ones.Soyuz: The Soyuz capsule has flown since the 1960s and still carries crews to the space station, making it the longest-serving crewed design.
Real spacecraft, not fictional ones.Hubble: Hubble launched in 1990 with a flawed mirror, and astronauts fixed it in 1993 with what amounted to corrective glasses.
Real spacecraft, not fictional ones.Curiosity: Curiosity landed on Mars in 2012 using a sky crane, and its wheels leave the letters JPL in Morse code in the dust.
Real spacecraft, not fictional ones.Vostok: Yuri Gagarin orbited Earth in Vostok 1 on 12 April 1961, a flight lasting about 108 minutes.
Real spacecraft, not fictional ones.Skylab: Skylab, the first US space station, fell back to Earth in 1979, scattering debris over Western Australia.
Real spacecraft, not fictional ones.Cassini: Cassini orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017 and ended by plunging into the planet to protect moons that might support life.
Real spacecraft, not fictional ones.New Horizons: New Horizons flew by Pluto in 2015 and revealed a huge heart-shaped glacier, nine years after launch.
Real spacecraft, not fictional ones.Lunar Module: The Lunar Module never needed to be streamlined since it flew only in vacuum, and Apollo 13's crew used it as a lifeboat.
Real spacecraft, not fictional ones.Millennium Falcon: The Millennium Falcon is from Star Wars, where Han Solo claims it made the Kessel Run in under twelve parsecs, a unit of distance, not time.
Real spacecraft, not fictional ones.TARDIS: The TARDIS is the Doctor's time machine in Doctor Who, whose name stands for Time And Relative Dimension In Space.
Real spacecraft, not fictional ones.Serenity: Serenity is the ship in the TV show Firefly, and it is fictional, as is its crew.
Real spacecraft, not fictional ones.Nostromo: The Nostromo is the doomed ship in Alien, and its name comes from a Joseph Conrad novel.
Real spacecraft, not fictional ones.Heart of Gold: The Heart of Gold is from The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, and runs on an Infinite Improbability Drive.
Real spacecraft, not fictional ones.Red Dwarf: Red Dwarf is a British sitcom's mining ship, and a red dwarf is also the most common kind of real star.
Real spacecraft, not fictional ones.Galactica: Galactica is the battleship in Battlestar Galactica, and it is fictional.
Real spacecraft, not fictional ones.X-wing: The X-wing is the Rebel starfighter in Star Wars, named for the shape of its wings.
Real spacecraft, not fictional ones.Planet Express: Planet Express is the delivery company's ship in Futurama, so it is cartoon.
Real spacecraft, not fictional ones.Thunderbird 3: Thunderbird 3 is the International Rescue rocket in the puppet series Thunderbirds, and it's not real.
Real spacecraft, not fictional ones.Death Star: The Death Star is a moon-sized battle station in Star Wars, and far bigger than any real spacecraft.
Real spacecraft, not fictional ones.Jupiter 2: Jupiter 2 is the family's ship in Lost in Space, and it's fictional.
Real spacecraft, not fictional ones.Star Destroyer: A Star Destroyer is an Imperial warship in Star Wars, and no such craft exists.

Things that usually have a propeller.Seaplane: Seaplanes have propellers and floats instead of wheels, and Alaska and the Maldives still rely on them as taxis.
Things that usually have a propeller.Biplane: The Wright brothers' first aircraft were biplanes, and their wooden propellers were carved to work like twisted wings.
Things that usually have a propeller.Submarine: Most submarines are driven by a single large propeller, shaped to be quiet, so enemy sonar can't hear them.
Things that usually have a propeller.Hovercraft: A hovercraft rides on a cushion of air, and big air propellers on top push it forward.
Things that usually have a propeller.Tugboat: Tugs have powerful propellers, often in swivelling pods, so they can push ships many times their size.
Things that usually have a propeller.Cruise ship: Most modern cruise ships use electric pods carrying propellers, which can rotate to steer the ship.
Things that usually have a propeller.Drone: A quadcopter drone's four spinning rotors are propellers, and each one adjusts speed to steer.
Things that usually have a propeller.Spitfire: The Spitfire's propeller was driven by a Rolls-Royce Merlin engine, and later versions used five blades for more power.
Things that usually have a propeller.Airboat: Airboats use a big aircraft-style propeller above the stern, which lets them glide over Florida's shallow Everglades.
Things that usually have a propeller.Blimp: Blimps are airships with propellers to push them forward, and the Goodyear blimps have been flying since the 1920s.
Things that usually have a propeller.Ferry: Most ferries use propellers; some fast ferries use water jets instead.
Things that usually have a propeller.Glider: Gliders have no engine; they stay up by riding rising air, and some have flown over 1,000 km.
Things that usually have a propeller.Hot air balloon: Balloons have no propeller: the pilot can only rise and fall, and winds do the rest of the steering.
Things that usually have a propeller.Rowboat: A rowboat is propelled by oars; in a sense, each oar acts like a propeller blade, but they aren't one.
Things that usually have a propeller.Canoe: Canoes are paddled, and have no propeller; the oldest known one, found in the Netherlands, is about 10,000 years old.
Things that usually have a propeller.Kayak: Kayaks are driven by a double-bladed paddle, and the Inuit built the original ones from seal skin stretched over frames.
Things that usually have a propeller.Bicycle: A bicycle is driven by pedals, not a propeller, though human-powered aircraft have flown across the English Channel with one.
Things that usually have a propeller.Sled: A sled is pulled over snow by dogs or gravity, and doesn't need a propeller.
Things that usually have a propeller.Jet ski: Jet skis use a water jet pump, which sucks in water and shoots it out the back, not a visible propeller.
Things that usually have a propeller.Rocket: Rockets work by expelling hot gas, which works even in space where a propeller would have nothing to push against.
Things that usually have a propeller.Skateboard: A skateboard is pushed by a foot, and so has no propeller.
Things that usually have a propeller.Bus: A bus has wheels driven by an engine; the only buses with propellers are amphibious ones.
Things that usually have a propeller.Hang glider: Hang gliders use no motor, and the pilot hangs beneath the wing and steers by shifting weight.
Things that usually have a propeller.Train: Trains run on rails with wheels, though some experimental ones, such as the Aérotrain, used a propeller.

Things in an office.Desk: A desk's name comes from the Latin for table, and the iconic Resolute desk in the Oval Office was made from timbers of a British ship.
Things in an office.Photocopier: Xerography was invented in 1938 and photocopiers took off in 1959, making the Xerox 914 an office revolution.
Things in an office.Water cooler: The gathering spot gave rise to the term 'water-cooler talk', and big bottles are often 5 gallons.
Things in an office.Cubicle: Robert Propst designed the Action Office at Herman Miller in 1960s and later regretted how his cube farms were used.
Things in an office.Filing cabinet: Vertical filing, popularized around 1900, replaced stacks of bundled papers, and Melvil Dewey's library tools helped spread card index systems.
Things in an office.Stapler: Staplers date to the 18th century, with one famously said to have been made for King Louis XV, each staple stamped with the court's emblem.
Things in an office.Whiteboard: Whiteboards were invented in the 1950s, but didn't catch on in offices until the 1990s when people mastered dry-erase markers.
Things in an office.Swivel chair: Thomas Jefferson is credited with an early swivel chair, a revolving seat he reportedly used while writing at his desk.
Things in an office.Printer: Laser printers use the same basic process as photocopiers, and the first one was built by Gary Starkweather at Xerox in the early 1970s.
Things in an office.Conference room: The big table in a conference room is often said to be what makes meetings last, and some firms test stand-up tables to speed them.
Things in an office.Reception desk: Receptionists are the first impression of a company, and the desk itself is designed to guide visitors with a welcoming look.
Things in an office.Hay bale: Hay is dried grass stored as feed, and a farm barn is its usual home, not a desk job.
Things in an office.Trough: A trough holds water or feed for animals, and it's a farm item; the word is also used for a low point in a wave or economy.
Things in an office.Anvil: Blacksmiths shape hot metal on an anvil, and the cartoon of an anvil dropping on a character is Looney Tunes slapstick.
Things in an office.Cauldron: Often linked to witches, it also originated as an ordinary cooking pot hung over fires in medieval kitchens.
Things in an office.Saddle: A saddle sits on a horse, and the word 'saddle' goes back to Old English, much older than any workplace chair.
Things in an office.Crib: Cribs are made for babies; their slat spacing is regulated, and the term 'crib sheet' for cheat notes is a different meaning of crib.
Things in an office.Bathtub: Bathtubs are for bathrooms; a famous legend says Archimedes shouted 'Eureka' in one, but it's no office furniture.
Things in an office.Pitchfork: A pitchfork is a farm tool for lifting hay, and the iconic 'American Gothic' painting holds one.
Things in an office.Harpoon: Harpoons are used for whaling or fishing and are made of barbed heads attached to a line, which wouldn't fit near a stapler.
Things in an office.Hospital bed: Adjustable beds let nurses raise a patient's head and knees, and the first such designs date to the early 1900s, so it's a ward item, not an office one.
Things in an office.Diving board: A diving board sits at a pool, and it's engineered to flex and spring a diver upward, rather than hold a desk.
Things in an office.Hammock: Hammocks were used by native peoples of the Caribbean and Central America, and Columbus brought them to Europe.
Things in an office.Stirrup: The stirrup supports a rider's foot, and its invention in Asia helped change cavalry warfare.

Things in a barber shop.Barber chair: Barber chairs can pump up and recline fully, and vintage cast-iron models from the 1900s are valued as collectibles.
Things in a barber shop.Clippers: Electric clippers were invented in the 1900s, and guard sizes make precise fades possible.
Things in a barber shop.Scissors: Haircutting scissors are sharpened to be razor fine, and one inch off hair takes only seconds with practiced hands.
Things in a barber shop.Razor: Straight razor shaves are the barber's classic craft, and traditional shops sharpen them on leather strops.
Things in a barber shop.Comb: Combs are among the oldest tools, with examples in archaeology dating back thousands of years.
Things in a barber shop.Mirror: Mirrors in barber shops are big enough to see yourself and the barber from the chair.
Things in a barber shop.Cape: The cape keeps hair clippings off the customer's clothes and is snapped at the neck.
Things in a barber shop.Barber pole: The red and white stripes recall the days when barbers also performed surgery and bloodletting; red for blood, white for bandages.
Things in a barber shop.Shaving cream: Barbers whip it into a rich lather with a brush to soften whiskers before shaving.
Things in a barber shop.Hot towel: Steaming towels open pores and soften the beard to make shaving smoother.
Things in a barber shop.Hair tonic: Old-fashioned hair tonics were rubbed into the scalp before it became fashionable to use pomade.
Things in a barber shop.Stethoscope: Invented in 1816 by Frenchman René Laennec, who rolled paper into a tube, it's a doctor's tool, not a barber's.
Things in a barber shop.Whisk: A whisk mixes eggs and sauces in kitchens, not lather in barber shops, where brushes are used instead.
Things in a barber shop.Anvil: An anvil is a blacksmith's tool, not a barber's, though barber surgeons did hammer a few things.
Things in a barber shop.Saddle: A saddle is horse tack, and a barber shop has no use for it.
Things in a barber shop.Ladle: Ladles are for soups and punch, not hair care; a barber's hot lather comes from a brush and bowl, not a scoop.
Things in a barber shop.Spatula: A spatula flips pancakes in a kitchen, not hair in a shop.
Things in a barber shop.Paint roller: Paint rollers belong in decorating, and the barber's cousin is the brush.
Things in a barber shop.Wrench: Wrenches tighten bolts, and a barber chair needs one only to be repaired.
Things in a barber shop.Microscope: The microscope is a laboratory tool, though a hair can look like a rope under one.
Things in a barber shop.Soldering iron: Soldering irons join metal wires, in electronics workshops rather than barbers'.
Things in a barber shop.Chisel: Chisels carve wood or stone, and barbers' sharpest tools are razors instead.
Things in a barber shop.Harpoon: A harpoon is a whaler's weapon, and wholly out of place at a barber's.
Things in a barber shop.Telescope: Telescopes look at stars, while a barber looks at the back of your head with a hand mirror.

Spooky creatures.Vampire: Bram Stoker's 1897 novel Dracula set the template, and the Count's name was borrowed from a Romanian ruler, Vlad.
Spooky creatures.Werewolf: Lycanthropy comes from the Greek lykos, wolf, and the idea of men turning into wolves goes back to ancient myth.
Spooky creatures.Mummy: Egyptian embalming took around 70 days, and the brain was pulled out through the nose.
Spooky creatures.Zombie: Rooted in Haitian vodou, where a zombie was a person revived by sorcery to work as a servant.
Spooky creatures.Ghost: In 1862, Pepper's ghost, a stage trick using angled glass, made see-through spirits appear to float on theater stages.
Spooky creatures.Witch: In Salem in 1692, twenty people were executed after witchcraft trials, nineteen by hanging.
Spooky creatures.Skeleton: An adult human has 206 bones; babies are born with about 300, which fuse as they grow.
Spooky creatures.Goblin: A mischievous creature of European folklore. In Tolkien's The Hobbit, goblins are cave-dwelling enemies.
Spooky creatures.Banshee: From Irish bean sidhe, woman of the fairy mound. Her wail is said to foretell a death in the family.
Spooky creatures.Ghoul: From Arabic ghul, a desert demon that robbed graves and ate the dead.
Spooky creatures.Poltergeist: German for noisy ghost, from poltern (to knock) and Geist (spirit), a spirit that hurls objects around.
Spooky creatures.Leprechaun: An Irish fairy cobbler said to guard a pot of gold. He is mischievous rather than frightening.
Spooky creatures.Cupid: The Roman god of desire. He is more cheerful than spooky, and early Greek Eros was a handsome youth, not a baby.
Spooky creatures.Elf: Norse alfar were powerful beings. The cute toy-making elf is a much later invention.
Spooky creatures.Easter Bunny: Arrived in America with German settlers, who told of an egg-laying hare called Osterhase.
Spooky creatures.Tooth Fairy: Her modern form took shape in the early 1900s in the US; older cultures had tooth customs like burying teeth.
Spooky creatures.Santa Claus: Based on Dutch Sinterklaas. Coca-Cola ads in the 1930s popularized his look but did not invent it.
Spooky creatures.Unicorn: Scotland's national animal, and gentle rather than scary in most stories.
Spooky creatures.Mermaid: Sailors' tales of them may have been inspired by manatees spotted at sea.
Spooky creatures.Fairy godmother: Cinderella's helper, popularized in Charles Perrault's 1697 version of the story, is kind, not spooky.
Spooky creatures.Snowman: Friendly, unlike the Abominable Snowman, which is the Yeti, the scary cousin.
Spooky creatures.Angel: From Greek angelos, meaning messenger, and a kind figure rather than a spooky one.
Spooky creatures.Cherub: In the Bible, cherubim are fearsome winged guardians, not chubby babies; Renaissance art changed their image.
Spooky creatures.Pegasus: Sprang from Medusa's blood when Perseus beheaded her, yet he is a hero's steed, not a monster.

Clothes for very cold weather.Parka: The word came into English from the Nenets language of Siberia, via Russian, where it meant animal skin.
Clothes for very cold weather.Mittens: Mittens are warmer than gloves because the fingers share heat in one pocket instead of being separated.
Clothes for very cold weather.Beanie: A close-fitting knit cap that pulls easily over the ears and was once a schoolboy's cap.
Clothes for very cold weather.Scarf: A scarf traps warm air around the neck, where heat escapes quickly, so it punches above its size.
Clothes for very cold weather.Thermals: Base layers trap body heat in a thin layer, and many are made of merino wool or synthetic fibers.
Clothes for very cold weather.Earmuffs: Chester Greenwood patented them in 1877, supposedly after inventing them as a teenager in Maine.
Clothes for very cold weather.Balaclava: Named after the Crimean War town of Balaclava, where British soldiers wore knitted head coverings in winter.
Clothes for very cold weather.Snow boots: Insulated, waterproof boots with deep treads, designed for ice and snow and usually lined with felt or fleece.
Clothes for very cold weather.Long johns: The name is often linked to boxer John L. Sullivan, who wore union suits, though the story is uncertain.
Clothes for very cold weather.Ski jacket: An insulated outer layer for the slopes, usually waterproof and breathable, with a hood and extra pockets.
Clothes for very cold weather.Down jacket: Filled with the soft underfeathers of ducks and geese, the lightest warm insulation, which loses its warmth when wet.
Clothes for very cold weather.Flip-flops: Japanese zori sandals inspired them, and the name imitates the slapping sound they make when you walk.
Clothes for very cold weather.Tank top: Named after tank suits worn in swimming pools, not military tanks, and now a hot-weather staple.
Clothes for very cold weather.Sundress: A light summer dress, made for warm days, and not suited to freezing weather.
Clothes for very cold weather.Bikini: Named after Bikini Atoll, where nuclear tests were held in 1946, the same year the swimsuit debuted.
Clothes for very cold weather.Board shorts: Long, loose shorts for surfing and beaches, designed to dry quickly, not for the cold.
Clothes for very cold weather.Sarong: A sarong is a wrapped cloth from Malay, worn in hot climates, so it fails the cold-weather test.
Clothes for very cold weather.Sun visor: A sun visor shades the eyes but leaves the top of the head open, which is why it is for warm weather.
Clothes for very cold weather.Espadrilles: From Catalan espardenya, from esparto grass, and a cord-soled summer shoe that is the opposite of snow boots.
Clothes for very cold weather.Linen shirt: Linen is made from flax and is light and breathable, so it's a summer fabric that fails in the cold.
Clothes for very cold weather.Crop top: A crop top ends above the waist, so it is no use in cold weather.
Clothes for very cold weather.Sandals: The oldest known sandals, found in Oregon, are about 10,000 years old, and they were made for warm weather.
Clothes for very cold weather.Panama hat: A Panama hat is made in Ecuador and is woven for shade, not warmth, and is a summer hat.
Clothes for very cold weather.Swim trunks: Swim trunks are designed for warm water, so they would not help in freezing weather.

Places with midnight sun in June.Tromso: This Norwegian city sees the sun stay up from about late May to late July, and in winter it has a polar night.
Places with midnight sun in June.Svalbard: The Norwegian archipelago has the sun up continuously from about 20 April to 23 August, and it hosts a vast seed vault.
Places with midnight sun in June.Utqiagvik: The northernmost town in the US, formerly Barrow, has no sunset for about 80 days in summer.
Places with midnight sun in June.Hammerfest: A Norwegian town above 70 degrees north, once among the first in Europe with electric street lights, with sun round the clock in summer.
Places with midnight sun in June.Longyearbyen: It is the main settlement of Svalbard, named after American John Munro Longyear, and the world's northernmost town of any size.
Places with midnight sun in June.Murmansk: The largest city north of the Arctic Circle, in Russia, has the sun up all day from late May to late July.
Places with midnight sun in June.Inuvik: This Canadian Arctic town is north of the Arctic Circle and has about 56 days of continuous daylight in summer.
Places with midnight sun in June.Kirkenes: A Norwegian town near the Russian border, where the sun does not set for about two months in summer.
Places with midnight sun in June.Alert: In Nunavut, it is the northernmost permanently inhabited place on Earth, a military station about 800 km from the North Pole.
Places with midnight sun in June.North Cape: A cliff on Norway's Arctic coast about 71 degrees north, long a tourist goal for the midnight sun.
Places with midnight sun in June.Anchorage: At about 61 degrees north, it is below the Arctic Circle, so the sun does set, though it stays up past 11pm in June.
Places with midnight sun in June.Oslo: Though far north, it is below the Arctic Circle, so June nights are just very short and bright, not truly sunlit.
Places with midnight sun in June.Helsinki: It has near-endless twilight in June, but it is south of the Arctic Circle, so the sun does dip below the horizon.
Places with midnight sun in June.Stockholm: June nights stay bright here with a few hours of twilight, but it is south of the Arctic Circle, so no true midnight sun.
Places with midnight sun in June.St. Petersburg: Famous for White Nights, when the sky stays light all night in June, but the sun does set, unlike inside the Arctic Circle.
Places with midnight sun in June.Edinburgh: The Scottish capital gets very long June days, but the sun sets in the late evening, so it has no midnight sun.
Places with midnight sun in June.Moscow: June days in Moscow are long, but the sun sets and no midnight sun occurs this far south.
Places with midnight sun in June.London: It gets about 16.5 hours of daylight in June, and the sun still sets well before midnight.
Places with midnight sun in June.Copenhagen: June days are long at about 17 hours of light, but the sun does set, since Denmark is far from the Arctic Circle.
Places with midnight sun in June.Sydney: It is winter there in June, with the shortest days of the year at about 10 hours of daylight.
Places with midnight sun in June.Cape Town: In June, it is deep winter in the southern hemisphere, with short days and the sun setting before 6pm.
Places with midnight sun in June.Juneau: Alaska's capital has long June days but sits well south of the Arctic Circle, so the sun does set.
Places with midnight sun in June.Dublin: It has very long June evenings, with light lingering past 11pm, but never a midnight sun.
Places with midnight sun in June.Seattle: At about 47 degrees north, it gets roughly 16 hours of daylight in June, far from the Arctic Circle.
